en: I bow to that Govinda, who is affectionate toward his devotees, by whose mere trace of grace the four aims of human life are attained;

I bow to my Guru, who is endowed with infinite qualities, who delights in infinite worship, who possesses infinite forms, and whose very nature is bliss. Indeed, in this world, the Blessed Sage Jaimini, out of supreme compassion, has investigated Dharma in twelve chapters, beginning with the words, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma."
In this context, *dharma* is an object that is enjoined with reference to a specific purpose (*prayojana*) by means of the Veda; for example, sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like.
For that [sacrifice] is enjoined with reference to heaven by such scriptural statements as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*). To explain further:

In the expression "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), there are two components: the injunctive portion and the suffix. Within that suffix, too, there are two components: the nature of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) and the nature of being an optative (*liṅtva*).
The nature of being a verbal suffix is found in all ten verbal suffixes (*lakāra*); however, the nature of being an optative exists only in the optative suffix itself.
In that context, by virtue of being both a verbal suffix (ākhyātatva) and an optative suffix (liṅtva), it is the *bhāvanā* alone that is expressed.
*Bhāvanā* is defined as a specific activity of an agent (*bhāvaka*) that is conducive to the bringing-into-being (*bhāvana*) of that which is to become (*bhavitṛ*).
And it is of two kinds: the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śābdī bhāvanā*) and the objective *bhāvanā* (*ārthī bhāvanā*).

In this context, the verbal *bhāvanā* is a specific operation (*vyāpāra*) of the expressive word that is conducive to human activity. And this is denoted by the element of the optative suffix (*liṅtva*); for when the optative suffix is heard, it is invariably cognized as: "This [suffix] impels me," or "This [suffix] possesses an operation conducive to my activity. And whatever is cognized from something is the denotation (*vācya*) of that thing, just as "cowness" (*gotva*) is the denotation of the word "cow."

And that specific activity conducive to engagement is, in the world, a particular intention residing in a person; however, in the Veda, due to the absence of a person, it resides solely in words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
For the Vedas are not composed by a person, because their study is uniform, just like the study [of the Vedas] today.

Since the non-human origin of the Vedas has been established by such arguments as these—according to the maxim "whatever cycle [of time] there is, that was preceded by a previous cycle"—and because saṃsāra is beginningless and the Lord is omniscient, it is sufficient for the purpose of this explanation to hold that the Lord, having remembered the Veda from a past cycle, teaches it in this present cycle. Since this much alone accounts for the matter, it is illogical to imagine that the Veda was composed after perceiving its meaning through some other means of knowledge.
Consequently, due to the absence of a [human] author, that [creative activity] resides solely in the word itself.
For this very reason, they designate it as "verbal creative activity" (śābdī bhāvanā).
And that verbal productive energy (*śābdī bhāvanā*) requires three factors:
the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*).

Among these, when there is an expectancy for the goal, the objective productive energy (*arthī bhāvanā*), which will be described as possessing its own three factors, is connected as the goal, because of the scriptural statement of common designation (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*) since both are understood from a single suffix.

Although the status of being cognizable by a single cognition is common even to the Sāṃkhya and other systems, nevertheless, because they are unfit [as means], there is no connection with them as that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*).
When there is an expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇa*), the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is connected as the instrument.

And its status as an instrument is not by way of producing the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), as in the case of sensory contact in the cognition of color and so forth; for if it were so, it would follow that the productive operation, which is a property of the word, would be non-existent prior to the cognition of the optative suffix, just as the cognition of color is non-existent prior to sensory contact. Rather, it is by way of bringing about the object to be brought about by the productive operation.

For the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth brings about the efficient-force of the meaning (*arthabhāvanā*), which is to be brought about by the verbal efficient-force (*śabdabhāvanā*), just as an axe brings about cutting.
Therefore, the cognition of the optative suffix and so forth is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
When there is an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the cognition of excellence (*prāśastya*) is connected as that very procedure.
And that knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) is produced by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity.

For those *arthavādas*, finding no purpose in conveying their own literal meaning, convey the excellence of the sacrifice through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because, if they were restricted solely to their own literal meaning, their lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) could not be avoided. Nor can this consequence be accepted; for since they are subsumed under the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), their lack of purpose is untenable.

For instance, the injunction for study, "The Veda is to be studied," while making known the duty to study the entire Veda, indicates that the whole Veda culminates in a purposeful meaning, because the study of something devoid of meaning is impossible. Furthermore, that Veda consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), mantras, names (*nāmadheya*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Among these, the injunction is purposeful by enjoining a meaningful object, and it enjoins an object not already established by other means.

For example, the injunction "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice" prescribes a purposeful oblation that was not previously established: "One should bring about heaven by means of the *agnihotra* oblation.
However, where an action is already established through another means, there is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) with reference to that action.

For instance, in the case of "One should offer with curd," since the oblation is already established by the rule "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," there is an injunction of curd alone with reference to the oblation: "One should effect the oblation by means of curd."
But where both [the general rule and the specific rule] have not been previously established, there he enjoins a qualified [rule].
As it has been said:
"If it is not taught by another"; the meaning is that "taught" (śiṣṭāḥ) means "instructed" (upadiṣṭāḥ).

For example, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), since neither the *soma* nor the sacrifice is previously established, there is an injunction of a sacrifice qualified by *soma*, meaning: "One should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessed of *soma*. Nor does this involve a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) from enjoining both [the substance and the action], because the qualified entity is a single unit. And in an injunction of a qualified entity, there is an indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); that is, by the word *soma*, the possessive sense is indicated, namely, "possessed of *soma*" (*somavatā*).
For indeed, without the indication of possessive meaning (matvarthalakṣaṇā), the syntactic connection of *soma* is not possible.

If, first of all, there were a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between *soma* and the sacrifice as a single form of instrument within the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), such that "one should effect the desired end by means of *soma* and by means of the sacrifice," then there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the injunction of two things. Furthermore, it would follow that *soma*, like the sacrifice, possesses primacy as the instrument for the productive activity toward the result; it would be impossible for the sacrifice to be for the sake of the *soma*; there would be no material substance (*dravya*) for the sacrifice; and there would be an impossibility of connecting *soma*—which is mentioned in a separate word—as the instrument, because the expectancy for an instrument in the productive activity toward the result expressed by the suffix is already satisfied by the sacrifice mentioned in the same word.

Furthermore, if there were a syntactic connection through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the connection would not be "by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena*) with respect to the Soma. This is because the sacrifice, which is presented within the same word and is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*) to the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix, cannot logically be connected to a separate efficient-force that has Soma as its object; moreover, it would follow that the sacrifice exists for the sake of the Soma. Nor is this an acceptable conclusion, as it would result in the postulation of two unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*). For the sacrifice’s being for the sake of the Soma cannot occur through a visible means, since no visible effect is produced in the Soma by the sacrifice, unlike the way threshing produces a visible effect in the rice grains.
Therefore, in that case, some invisible effect (*adṛṣṭa*) must be produced by the Soma, just as [an invisible effect] is produced in the rice grains by the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

Likewise, if the sacrifice has the Soma as its purpose, it must be stated that the Soma is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the fruit. And it has been stated that being the instrument of an efficient-force consists in bringing about the object to be realized by that efficient-force.

Furthermore, Soma is not capable of producing a result without an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), because it is reduced to ashes by the oblation enjoined by the sentence "he offers with the cups" (*grahair juhoti*). Consequently, since two unseen forces would result, the sacrifice cannot have Soma as its purpose; thus, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) "one should bring Soma into being by means of the sacrifice" is not possible. Moreover, it is logically untenable for Soma, which is presented as the instrument (*karaṇa*), to be construed as the objective to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Now, the positive syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "One should bring about the sacrifice by means of *soma*. In this regard, although the visible purpose—the accomplishment of the sacrifice—is obtained because *soma* serves the sacrifice as its instrument (*karaṇa*), there is no resulting in two unseen effects (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor is there an impossibility of connecting *soma*, which is presented as the instrument, with the status of being the goal (*sādhya*), since it is connected precisely as the instrument. Nevertheless, because [the sacrifice] has not yet been established, the impossibility of connecting the sacrifice—which is already connected as the instrument of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—with the status of being the goal remains exactly as it was.

If it is objected: "In the expression *yajeta* ('one should sacrifice'), the sacrifice (*yāga*) is presented neither as an instrument (*karaṇa*) nor as an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because there is no instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) to express that. Rather, only the mere relation of the sacrifice to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is perceived. And the relation of the sacrifice to the productive activity can occur both as an instrument and as an end to be accomplished. In that regard, by taking the aspect of instrumentality, there would be a connection with the fruit (*phala*); and by taking the aspect of being the end to be accomplished, there would be a connection with the accessory (*guṇa*)."—if this is argued:
It is not so.

Even though through the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) only a mere relationship between the sacrifice and the result is understood, nevertheless, at the stage when [the sacrifice] is presented as the instrument (*karaṇa*), its presentation as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is impossible, because of contradiction and the resulting occurrence of two mutually opposed functions.

Therefore, once the connection as an instrument has necessarily occurred—namely, "one should bring about heaven by means of the sacrifice"—thereafter, the connection as the end to be accomplished must be stated, namely, "one should bring about the sacrifice by means of the *soma*."
Consequently, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Nor is it reasonable to say that the mere nature of the sacrifice (*yāgasvarūpa*) connects with the nature of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the suffix; for it is only the factors of action (*kāraka*) that connect with an action (*kriyā*).

Thus it is established that for *soma*, neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice is possible. If it is objected: "In the case of *yajeta* ('one should sacrifice'), when the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix has a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), the sacrifice is construed as the instrument; likewise, when there is a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), let *soma* be construed within that very productive urge as the procedure. Thus, there is no need for the figurative indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). This is not so. Because the instrumental case-ending in *somena* expresses instrumentality, it does not denote that *soma* is the procedure.

If "the state of being a procedure" (*itikartavyatātva*) is expressed here through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then it is better to assume a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in the word *soma* itself, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*), according to the maxim: "But when a quality [is to be enjoined], it is improper to assume [an additional] meaning."

Now, if it is argued that—according to the principle of "contradiction arising from what has been established" (*saṃjātavirodhatva*) as stated in the section beginning with "Or rather, [the Veda] because of the observation of the majority" (*prāyadarśanāt*)—the definition applies only to the final cognition (*pratyaya*), even so, there is no logical connection of *soma* as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*); for an already established entity cannot possess the nature of a procedure, since only an action possesses the nature of a procedure, whereas a substance is merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*). Precisely because of this lack of the nature of a procedure, a substance is not grasped through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
As they say:

"Except through connection with an intermediate action fashioned by the sentence, the contextual actions do not take up qualities or substances by means of the requirements of manner (*kathaṃbhāva*). We shall explain this further below. Moreover, in the case of "One should sacrifice with *soma*," this is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the sacrifice, not the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravākya*); for "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*" is the injunction of qualification.

Furthermore, in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*). This is because such an expectancy does not clearly arise, being obscured by the expectancy for a specific desired result (*iṣṭaviśeṣakāṅkṣā*).
Thus it is established that *soma* is not connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as its procedure.

Therefore, since connection [of the substance] is impossible within a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), one must necessarily resort to the figurative indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in the verbal expression.

But even so, in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma," there is no injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), because that would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) and because it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
Rather, let it be an injunction of a mere accessory (*guṇamātra*), as in "he offers oblation with curd," since the injunctive power (*vidhiśakti*) transfers to the accessory. As they say:

"When another word is heard connected with a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) everywhere, the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) transfers [to that word], and thus the verbal root becomes a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Nor should it be argued that because the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not already established, Soma cannot be enjoined with reference to it; for the sacrifice is already established by the text: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Nor should it be argued that because this is an injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), it cannot be an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*); for, as in the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Udbhid," it is logically possible for a single sentence to function as both types of injunction.
And thus, in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma," there is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
For if this were a prescription of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), then, due to the impossibility of syntactic connection, there would be an indication of possessive meaning.
However, in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," when the sacrifice itself is being prescribed, there is nowhere an indication of possessive meaning.

First of all, this is not the case in the sentence [“One should bring about heaven by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice”], because the name-word is construed through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) itself as: “one should bring about heaven by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
Nor is it the case in the sentence “One should sacrifice with Soma,” because Soma is enjoined with reference to the sacrifice, as in: “one should bring about the sacrifice by means of Soma.
But surely, even in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is the figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, it has been said:

"Whether in an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the sacrifice is intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*); that which stands near it in the instrumental case does not lose its status as denoting that [instrument].

And thus, if it is argued that even in an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), just as in an injunction of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is indeed the implication of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—
It is not so;
for it is only when the connection with the quality (*guṇa*) is otherwise impossible that the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is accepted.

However, when the sentence [expressing] the result (*bhāvya-vākya*) involves the connection of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇa*), then that indication must be accepted due to the impossibility of such a connection [otherwise].

Furthermore, in the case of an injunction regarding a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*), there is no syntactic connection of the root-meaning as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because there is no evidence for it.

For in the sentence "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the homa is not heard to have the status of an instrument; this is because there is an absence of the third case ending or other markers that would express it.

If it is argued that [the instrumental status] is to be inferred, we say no; since the subordinate element is what is intended to be enjoined there, when there is an expectancy for something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is more appropriate to assume its status as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, the sense is: "One should effect the homa by means of curd."

Furthermore, there is no such rule that in the context of *bhāvanā*, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) must be construed solely as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not in any other manner; for if it were so, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the first section of the sixth book would fail to arise. In that prima facie argument, regarding passages such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), it is suspected—on the basis of the direct syntactic connection within the same word—that the sacrifice (*yāga*) might be the objective (*bhāvya*) in relation to the *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix which refers to the act of sacrificing; this suspicion is then refuted on the grounds that [the sacrifice] is not an end of human life (*apuruṣārthatva*).

Furthermore, if the meaning of the verbal root were connected to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) solely as an instrument (*karaṇa*), then the very suspicion that it might be the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) would not arise; thus, the first section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya-prathama-pāda*) would become redundant. Moreover, in the *Vājapeyādhikaraṇa*, a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*) was raised and refuted; if the meaning of the verbal root were connected solely as an instrument, the suspicion of a simultaneous connection would not even exist.
The connection between the Tantras and the resolution of doubts have also been explained.

Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root does not connect solely as the instrument (*karaṇa*); for it has been stated in the section concerning desires for qualities (*guṇakāmādhikaraṇa*) that the meaning of the verbal root connects as the locus (*āśraya*). To explain:
Regarding the injunction, "One desiring sensory power should offer curd," the oblation (*homa*) is not being enjoined here, because it has already been enjoined by another statement.

Nor is the connection between the oblation and the fruit being enjoined, because that would render the word expressing the accessory (*guṇa-pada*) meaningless. Nor does it enjoin a connection between the accessory and the fruit, because that would render the word expressing the fruit (*phala-pada*) meaningless.

Nor does it enjoin a connection between both [the substance and the deity], because when an action is already established, enjoining multiple things would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). As they say:
"When an action is already established, more than one accessory (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined; but when it is not yet established, even many may be enjoined by a single effort."

And here, the mention of "quality" (*guṇa*) is merely illustrative, just like the mention of "action" (*karman*); for when multiple things are enjoined with reference to a single object, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

It is for this very reason that in the section concerning the singularity of the cup (*grahaikatvādhikaraṇa*), it is stated that in the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), since there would be a syntactical split if both the singularity and the cleansing were enjoined with reference to the cup, the singularity of the cup is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

And in the *Revatyadhikaraṇa*, it is stated: regarding the passage, "Having made the *vāravantīya* the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon these very *revatī* verses, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this," since the connection of the *vāravantīya* with the *revatī* verses, its connection with the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, and its connection with the fruit are all being enjoined, there would be a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, rather than [the *bhāvanā*] being subordinate to another *bhāvanā*, a distinct *bhāvanā* is enjoined. Thus it was said.

Therefore, since the oblation (*homa*) is already established, it is not possible to enjoin both [the oblation and the material] simultaneously; nor is another oblation enjoined, because that would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), the abandonment of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtahāna*), and the assumption of something not under discussion (*aprakṛtakalpanā*). Furthermore, it would entail the fallacy of implying a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Nor is it correct to say that curd alone is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*), for it is impossible for that which is isolated and not engaged in an operation to function as an instrument, given that being an instrument is necessarily defined by its being pervaded by the activity of an agent.

If it is asked, "What then is enjoined? [the answer is: by the instrumental case ending in the word *dadhnā* ("with curd"), the curd, which has been introduced as the substratum (*karaṇa*), is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the efficient-force toward the fruit (*phala-bhāvanā*). This is because, as the meaning of the suffix, the curd possesses primacy.
Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should effect the sense-faculty (*indriya*) by means of the curd as the substratum.
And when there arises the expectation, "With respect to what does this instrumentality exist?", the oblation (*homa*), obtained through proximity (*saṃnidhi*), serves as the locus (*āśraya*).
It is connected with that [agenthood]; and thus, the connection of the meaning of the verbal root as the substratum is established.
Let us now return to the subject at hand.
Thus it is established that the meaning of the verbal root does not connect solely as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
What then? In some cases it connects as an instrument, in some as an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and in some as a locus (*āśraya*).
This is the case in the injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*).
Since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is possible precisely by taking [the word] as a substance, there is no need for the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, if it were a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) involving the indication of possessive meaning, one must state what the authority (*māna*) is for the quality being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*).

First of all, it is not *śruti* (direct Vedic statement). For if there were a *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of the possessive sense), then the *śruti* would serve as the authority for the action being subordinate to the possessor (*matvartha*) alone, and not for the quality (*guṇa*) being subordinate either.

If it is argued that a sentence (*vākya*) is merely co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra-mātra*), does that constitute an independent means of knowledge? Or does it do so by postulating an indicative power (*liṅga*) and a direct statement (*śruti*)? It cannot be the first, because it would contradict the section on relative strength (*balābalādhikaraṇa*). For in that section, it was stated that a sentence serves as the authority for subordination only after it has postulated an indicative power and a direct statement.

In the second case, having set aside the directly perceived scripture (*pratyakṣā śruti*), one would be resorting to a futile effort by either postulating another scripture or postulating a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of that very same one. And such reliance [on another scripture] occurs only as a last resort (*agatyā*) in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Furthermore, let us grant for the sake of argument the postulation of another scripture.

Nevertheless, does the directly perceived injunction itself, assisted by that [word], enjoin the accessory as being subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root, or is it a separate, inferred injunction?
If you say "an inferred one," no; for that would result in the direct injunction becoming purposeless.

For at that time, no quality (guṇa) is enjoined by it, because one accepts another assumed injunction; nor is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) [enjoined], since that is already enjoined by another statement.
Now, the very injunction being heard, accompanied by an assumed scriptural text, [enjoins] the verbal root...

If it is argued that [the sentence] prescribes the quality (*guṇa*) as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the ritual action (*artha*), then how does the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) connect there?

If you say "as the instrument" (*karaṇatvena*), we say no, because such a connection is untenable; for a connection such as "by means of curd, by means of the oblation" (*dadhnā homena*) is not possible.

The connection [of the material] occurs solely as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). If it is argued that "one should effect the oblation by means of curd" (*dadhnā homaṃ bhāvayet*), this is not so; for if that were the case, even in a restatement (*anuvāda*), the meaning of the verbal root would have to be connected only as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and thus that [established principle] would be disregarded. Furthermore, the intended meaning of the sentence would have to be accepted even without the figurative indication of possessive significance (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, there is no figurative indication of possessive significance in the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
As for the *Vārttika* passage, "Whether in an injunction or in a restatement," that is based on the surface appearance (*pratīti*) and not on the actual state of things (*vastugati*).

For instance, as long as the sentence "one should offer the Agnihotra" is not taken into account, and only the sentence "one offers with curd" is considered, then for those who—by means of the logic of the sixth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]—recognize that the oblation (*homa*) is not the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*), and whose internal organs are permeated by the impressions of the *pratipadādhikaraṇa* and the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, there arises such a thought: "One should effect the desired end by means of an oblation characterized by curd."

For in the section on the *pratipadādhikaraṇa*, regarding injunctions such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), a doubt arises as to whether both the accessory (*guṇa*) and the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) are connected as instruments (*karaṇa*) for the production of the result (*phalabhāvanā*), or whether only one is so connected. Having raised the objection that all of them might be connected as instruments for the production of the result—on the grounds that they all equally attain a connection with the primary element and because there is no decisive factor [to choose otherwise]—it is stated that, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), only one is the instrument for the production of the result. For being an instrument for the production of the result consists in bringing about that which is to be produced (*bhāvya*) by that production; and since that which is to be produced, such as heaven, cannot exist without an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating multiple unseen potencies if multiple things were taken as instruments.

Therefore, there is instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) for only one [of the two]. Even when there is only one, a doubt arises in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* as to whether the instrumentality of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) belongs to the substance (*dravya*) and the quality (*guṇa*), or rather to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Having raised the objection that the instrumentality of the efficient force belongs to the substance and the quality alone, on the basis of the principle that "that which is already accomplished (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*bhavya*"), it is stated that the instrumentality of the efficient force belongs to the meaning of the verbal root alone, because the direct hearing of the word (*padaśruti*) is more powerful.

And thus, it is established that when one has not yet considered other sentences, even in the case of an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), there arises the suspicion that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*); consequently, there is a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in the word denoting the accessory.

However, when the other sentence enjoining the oblation, "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), is taken into account, then since the oblation has already been enjoined by that other sentence, only the accessory is enjoined with reference to that [already established] oblation. Thus, upon such consideration, there is no possessive indication.

For this very reason, it was stated by Pārthasārathi Miśra in the section on the Āghāra and Agnihotra: "This is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi) by way of its result, not as a primary injunction.

Alternatively, this Vārttika intends to refer to an injunction of qualification (adhikāravidhi), because [in cases such as] "one should sacrifice with the Udbhid," there is a qualification [of the agent]. For in that case, either the sacrifice itself is enjoined, or it is restated as already established by the originative injunction (utpattivākya). In either case, since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is construed as the instrument (karaṇa), the word ending in the third case denotes that [instrument]; otherwise, the syntactical connection would be untenable.

Therefore, since the syntactic connection is established even without *lakṣaṇā* when there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is no need for the *matvarthalakṣaṇā*. Consequently, in the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is no injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), but rather an injunction of the quality alone. It is more reasonable, however, that the sacrifice itself is enjoined in the sentence "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta*); otherwise, the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* would result. To this, it is replied:

Even if there is no indication of possessive implication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) when Soma is enjoined with reference to a sacrifice, nevertheless, because the sacrifice is not yet established, it is not possible to enjoin Soma with reference to a sacrifice in the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*).

Nor can it be argued that since the sacrifice is already established by such injunctions as "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma," only a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined with reference to it; for that [injunction] is an injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*), and thus it cannot logically function as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*).

An originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is one that makes known merely the essential nature of a ritual action (*karman*). And for a ritual action enjoined by such an injunction, the connection with a specific result is established solely by the qualification injunction (*adhikāravidhi*), because the status of being a qualification injunction consists precisely in making known the connection with a specific result. For example, the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*) enjoins only the connection with a specific result for the ritual action enjoined by the [originative injunction] "That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*yad āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālo bhavati*). Thus, it is a qualification injunction, not an originative injunction.

This cannot be so; for it is not possible for the statement "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*) to be an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*). This is because the sentences beginning with "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*) would then become redundant; for in that case, the ritual action would not be enjoined by them, since it would have already been enjoined by the statement "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Nor is it possible for them to be injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhāna*), because enjoining multiple accessories regarding an action already established would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, it is logical that "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" is the originative injunction, while "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" is the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).

If it is argued that even if the injunction *jyotiṣṭomena* is accepted as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*)—similar to *udbhidā yajeta paśukāmaḥ* and other such rules—there is no pointlessness for anything; and since *somena yajeta* is a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because only soma is enjoined with reference to the sacrifice—this is not so.

Even though there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), nevertheless, in the sentence "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma," since both the essential nature of the rite and its connection to the fruit are being enjoined, there is indeed a syntactical split characterized by prolixity (*gaurava*); for such a split does not exist when only the connection to the fruit is enjoined for the rite already established by the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma. However, in the case of "one should sacrifice with the Udbhid," because there is no other scriptural injunction [establishing the rite], one must resort to that [prolixity] as there is no other way.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) as well, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because both the nature of the ritual action and its accessory (*guṇa*) are being enjoined; for the accessory is not enjoined by the directly heard injunction itself, since the injunction of the qualifier is merely implied (*ārthika*).
Indeed, in every instance of an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the injunction of the qualifier is implied.

However, if the phrase "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*jyotiṣṭomena*) were an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), then both the nature of the ritual action and its connection to the fruit [would have to be enjoined].

Thus, both [the injunction and the qualification] must be enjoined by the very same directly stated injunction; this constitutes a firm "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*), characterized by excessive weightiness.
As they say:
"When words are made to refer to a sacrifice that is [only] indirectly implied (*śrauta-yāga-upamānitve*), there is an extreme weightiness."
It cannot be argued that, because the powers (*vasitā*) are expressed by a single statement, there is no contradiction in the implication of further meanings;

nor can it be said that, although there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) if it were an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), there would nevertheless still be a possessive compound indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). This is because such indication is indeed accepted [in this context], for syntactical split is a more inferior fault than indication.
For *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is a fault of the word (*pada*), whereas *vākyabheda* (splitting of the sentence) is a fault of the sentence (*vākya*);

because between a word and a sentence, it is more appropriate to attribute a fault to the word alone, according to the maxim: "In the case of a quality, an improper attribution [of a fault] is not to be made."

For this very reason, regarding the statement "one who has a son and has black hair should establish the sacred fires," it has been said that since there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if one were to enjoin both "having a son" and "having black hair" as attributes of the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*), the two words instead indicate a particular stage of life through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, when a syntactical split is entailed, secondary implication must indeed be accepted. Consequently, the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) alone is the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), and not "one [should sacrifice] with the Jyotiṣṭoma. This is because the latter would entail the faults of prolixity (*gaurava*) and syntactical split due to secondary implication.

Furthermore, in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), if the injunction were for the sacrifice itself, it would be an injunction of the primary meaning of the word (*śrutyartha-vidhāna*); however, if it were an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇa-vidhāna*), it would be an injunction of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-vidhāna*). And that is improper when an injunction of the primary meaning of the word is possible.
As they say:
"A sentence whose meaning is vast [in scope] is [only used] when an injunction of the primary meaning of the word is not possible."
The meaning is that the meaning of the sentence is the meaning of another word.

Even in the case of "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma," since it is the sacrifice itself that is enjoined with reference to the fruit, there is no injunction of the meaning of the entire sentence; for even those who accept it as an originative injunction (utpattividhi) admit this very point.
Therefore, "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" is indeed an injunctive statement of qualification (adhikāravidhi).
Furthermore, an injunction regarding the essential nature of an action (karmasvarūpavidhi) is to be accepted only where the form of that action is perceived;
and the sacrifice has two forms: the material substance and the deity.

In the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), although no deity is perceived—because the Soma-sacrifice is unmanifest, and its unmanifest nature consists in the absence of a deity enjoined for its own sake—nevertheless, a substance is indeed perceived; by means of that substance, the essential form of the sacrifice can certainly be known. This is because, despite the absence of a primary deity, there exist deities for the various vessels (*graha*) prescribed by such sentences as "To Soma, to the Aśvins, to Viṣṇu," and since the assistance to the sacrifice is rendered incidentally even by these deities intended for the vessels, the nature of the sacrifice remains ascertainable.

In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," neither a material substance nor a deity is heard. Therefore, if this were an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), there would be the following deficiency: there would be no knowledge of a specific sacrifice, because a general sacrifice cannot be enjoined and only a specific one can be enjoined. For this reason, this is not an originative injunction of a ritual action (*karmotpattividhi*). [Objection: Even so, the injunction "He offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*) would also not be an originative injunction of the *homa*, because its form (*rūpa*) is not heard therein; and since that [form] is heard in "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the latter alone would have to be the originative injunction.
And in that case, there would be a contradiction with the section concerning the *āghāra* and *agnihotra*.

For in that [section], it was stated that "he offers the *agnihotra*" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*) is an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), while "he offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and so forth are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). If this is argued, [the reply is: True. Although no ritual form (*rūpa*) is perceived in "he offers the *agnihotra*"—since the word *agnihotra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) by the principle of "being mentioned along with that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*)—we shall explain this further on. Nevertheless, its status as an originative injunction is accepted, because otherwise it would result in meaninglessness (*anarthakyāpatti*).
And the injunction "he offers with curd" does not become purposeless, because it is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi).
Therefore, it is logical that "he performs the Agnihotra" is the originative injunction (utpattividhi) of the rite.
Furthermore, the injunction "by means of the Jyotiṣṭoma" does not become purposeless, since it is established as an injunction of qualification (adhikāravidhi).

Therefore, for what reason should that [injunction of the object] be accepted in a sentence devoid of it, when it is already possible in a sentence possessing form? Furthermore, if "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) were an origin-injunction (*utpattividhi*) of this rite, then "He offers with milk" (*payasā juhoti*) could not enjoin milk as a distinct alternative for this same rite; for the expectancy is already satisfied by the quality enjoined at the time of origin, and no other quality can be enjoined in a case where the requirement has been occupied by a quality enjoined at the time of origin. This is because the expectancy is fulfilled by that very quality enjoined at the time of origin.

Therefore, even that [view] would require the injunction of another distinct action characterized by those qualities; and thus there would be the burden of postulating multiple unseen potencies (*adṛṣṭa*). However, if "He offers the Agnihotra" is taken as an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), then when the action enjoined by this sentence requires a substance, the qualities are enjoined simultaneously—by way of the "pigeons on a threshing floor" maxim—with such sentences as "He offers with curd" and "He offers with milk. Thus, there is no burden of postulating multiple unseen potencies.

Therefore, it is logical that "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" is the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), while "He sacrifices with milk" and similar statements are injunctions of accessories (*guṇavidhi*). However, in the case of "One should sacrifice with *soma*," there is no defect whatsoever in accepting this sentence—which possesses a specific ritual form—as the originative injunction of the rite; for in both positions, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting is equal. Consequently, it is correct that "One should sacrifice with *soma*" is indeed the originative injunction itself. Enough, then, with this reflection on the detailed exposition concerning the determination of injunctions.
Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus it is established that an injunction (vidhi) prescribes a purposeful matter not otherwise obtained [by other means].
And that injunction is of four kinds.

[The injunctions are] the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi), the applicatory injunction (viniyoga-vidhi), the procedural injunction (prayoga-vidhi), and the qualification injunction (adhikāra-vidhi).
Among these, the originative injunction is that which makes known merely the essential nature of the ritual act; for example, "He performs the Agnihotra oblation.
And in the originative injunction, the ritual act is construed as being the instrument (karaṇa).
One should contemplate the desired end (*iṣṭa*) by means of the oblation (*homa*), but not [contemplate] the oblation itself as the goal to be accomplished.

For if that were the case, since a thing already to be accomplished cannot be connected with another thing to be accomplished, there would be no connection with the fruit understood from the sentence of qualification (*adhikārāvākya*).

However, when there is a syntactic connection [of the oblation] as an instrument (*karaṇatva*), one should contemplate the desired end by means of the oblation; and when the expectancy arises as to "what is that desired end?", the connection with a specific fruit becomes possible.

Nor should it be argued that, because there is no word denoting a desired object in the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), how can the meaning of the sentence be "one should effect the desired [result] through the ritual act" (*karmaṇeṣṭaṃ bhāvayet*)? For the very hearing of the injunctive suffix (*vidhiśruti*) itself conveys the desired object;
for, impelling the person toward a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it makes known merely the connection between the ritual act and its fruit.
Therefore, it is correct that in the originative injunction, the ritual act is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For this very reason, in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the word *udbhid* ending in the third case is appropriate; for the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) "one should effect the desired [result] by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice" is possible. Even for those [grammarians] for whom the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the state of being a means to the desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), the connection of nouns ending in the third case as instruments is likewise impossible.

For it is not possible [to say], "the sacrifice is the means to the desired, [and] by the *udbhid*"; because an instrumental factor denoted by the third case, which is incapable of connecting with gender or number, connects only with the verb.

[Objection: But even for you, in the originative injunctions of rituals such as "He offers the Agnihotra," the connection of the objects denoted by words ending in the accusative case is untenable; for it is not possible [to say], "One should effect the Agnihotra by means of the oblation.

[Reply: True; however, the accusative case that is actually heard is a restatement (anuvāda) of the status of being an end (sādhyatva), which is already implied by the sense. For since the oblation is connected as the instrument (karaṇa), and since that which is not itself established cannot function as an instrument, that accusative case—when its primary syntactic connection is blocked—indicates the sense of the instrumental case, as in the expression "He offers barley-meal" (*śaktūñ juhoti*).
Pārthasārathi Miśra has stated: "One should effect the desired result by means of the Agnihotra oblation.
Therefore, it is not at all untenable for nouns ending in the accusative case to be connected as names of the ritual acts (*karman*).
Thus it is established that in the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), the ritual act is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The injunction that makes known the relationship between a subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna) is the injunction of application (viniyogavidhi).

For example: "One offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*). For this [injunction] prescribes the connection of the curd—which has attained the status of a subsidiary through the instrumental case ending—with the oblation, as in: "One should effect the oblation by means of curd."

And the auxiliaries of this injunction (*vidhi*) are the six means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), consisting of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*). By means of the injunction assisted by these, subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*)—which consists in being pervaded by an activity directed toward another and is synonymous with "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*)—is made known. Among these, a direct statement is an independent utterance.
And that [injunction] is threefold: the enjoiner (*vidhātṛ*), the designator (*abhidhātṛ*), and the applicator (*viniyoktṛ*).
Among these, the enjoiner consists of [the suffixes] *liṅ* and so forth;
the designator is the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) concerning rice and other materials.
That word by the mere hearing of which a relationship is understood is the *viniyoktrī* (the enjoining word).
It is threefold:
consisting of an inflectional ending (*vibhakti*), consisting of co-occurrence in the same expression (*samānābhidhāna*), and consisting of being a single word (*ekapada*).

In that context, subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) is established by the hearing of a case-ending (*vibhaktiśruti*). For example, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), the subsidiarity of the rice-grains to the sacrifice is established by the hearing of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*).

It should not be argued that the subsidiarity of the rice-grains cannot be established because the sacrifice has already been restricted by the cake (*puroḍāśa*) prescribed in the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*); for [the rice] serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the cake. Just as the animal (*paśu*) is subsidiary to the sacrifice by being the material cause of the heart and other organs which constitute the oblation (*havis*), so too is the rice-grain subsidiary by being the material cause of the cake.

Nor should it be argued: "Why could the animal itself not be the direct subsidiary (aṅga)? For that [animal] is slaughtered, whereas the heart and other organs are what are actually being offered. Indeed, that which is being offered is the oblation (havis), just like the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and so forth;
for there is the scriptural injunction: "He cuts off from the middle and from the front half."
Furthermore, the heart and other organs being cut off do not constitute the animal itself, because of the scriptural statement: "He cuts off first from the heart.
Therefore, only the heart and the other organs are the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*); the animal, however, is the material cause (*prakṛtidravya*).

But in the *pātnīvata* sacrifice, the animal itself is directly the constituent part (*aṅga*), since there is an injunction for its release while it is still alive: "Having carried fire around it, he releases the *pātnīvata* animal."
Where there is a "multitude-slaughterer" (tūparapaśu), it is established that the animal (*paśu*) is the primary substance (*prakṛtidravya*).

Likewise, rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) are also a subsidiary element of the sacrifice by virtue of being the primary substance, as indicated by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in the instrumental case. Similarly, even the purchase (*kraya*) is a subsidiary element [of the ritual] by virtue of the instrumental scriptural statement.

Nor should it be argued that, being formless, such [time] cannot be a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the purchase; for its status as a subsidiary is established by way of delimiting the substance in the form of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*).
Just as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), the sprinkling is a subsidiary of the rice-grains due to the direct statement of the accusative case.

And that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is not for the sake of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the rice grains; for it would be purposeless with respect to that nature, since there is no impossibility of the rice grains' nature existing without sprinkling. Rather, it is prompted by its being a means to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). If the sprinkling is performed upon the rice grains, then when the sacrifice is accomplished by means of them, the *apūrva* comes into being, and not otherwise.

Therefore, by the force of the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā-śruti*) assisted by the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is stated that the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) belongs to the sprinkling insofar as it is a means to that *apūrva* which results from the production of the rice-grain meal and the subsequent vitalization of the offering.
In this way, it should be understood that all auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are likewise applied through *apūrva*.

Similarly, in the case of the rule "With the mantra 'He has grasped this rein of Order,' he takes the horse's halter," the mantra’s status as an auxiliary to the horse’s halter is established by the direct hearing of the accusative case-ending.
As for the claim that this application is based on syntactical connection (*vākya*), that is not correct.

That being the case, since indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*), as soon as [the mantra] would become an auxiliary to the horse-haltering-rope (*aśvābhidhānī*) by virtue of syntactical connection, it would instead—by virtue of its indicative power—become an auxiliary to the rope in general, just as the mantra "I make a pleasant seat for thee" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) is an auxiliary to the act of preparing the seat.

However, in the case of a scriptural application (*śrautaviniyoga*), as soon as the possibility of the mantra being subsidiary to the mere rope arises from its indicative power (*liṅga*), it is superseded by direct statement (*śruti*). Just as in the passage "With the *aindrī* [verse] he worships the *gārhapatya* fire," the third-case direct statement establishes that the *aindrī* verse is subsidiary to the worship of the *gārhapatya*, so too here the application is made to the horse's halter; thus, it is logical that the mantra is subsidiary to the horse's halter.

Therefore, this application is indeed scriptural (*śrauta*), just as the status of the *āhavanīya* fire as subsidiary to the oblation is established by the seventh-case direct statement in the rule "He offers in the *āhavanīya*."
In this manner, other applications [of words] through the hearing of case-endings (vibhakti-śruti) are also to be understood.

In the statement "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), singularity and masculinity are subordinate to the factor of action (kāraka) by virtue of the hearing of co-referential expression (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*); the number expressed by the verbal suffix in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is subordinate to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of the hearing of co-referential expression, and it is subordinate to the sacrifice itself by virtue of the hearing of being within the same word (*ekapada-śruti*). Nor should it be asked how that [number], being formless, can be subordinate to the sacrifice; for its applicability is established through the mediation of delimiting the agent (*kartṛ-pariccheda*).
And the agent is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).
For by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is expressed; and since that [force] is untenable without an agent, it implies one.
Now, why is it described in this way—that the agent is obtained through implication?
Why could the agent not be directly denoted by the verbal suffix itself? For when the verbal suffix is heard, the agent is perceived just as the efficient force is.

Nor is it correct to argue that since the *bhāvanā* can be implied [by another word], there is no need to postulate that it is denoted by [the verbal suffix]; for if that were the case, then since the agent (*kartṛ*) denoted by the verbal suffix itself could imply the *bhāvanā*, the suffix would likewise not denote it. Furthermore, the *bhāvanā* is not connected with the agent alone, as it is also connected with other factors of action (*kāraka*).
Therefore, because there is no distinguishing factor, it would not immediately imply the agent alone.

The agent, however, is connected only with the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) and not with any other *kāraka* (grammatical factor). According to the principle that "since subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no mutual connection between equals," the agent immediately implies that *bhāvanā*. Therefore, it is the agent alone that is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Why, then, should the *bhāvanā* not be obtained through implication rather than being directly expressed?

Furthermore, if this were the case, the third and subsequent case endings would likewise not denote the instrument and so forth, since they too could be obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*), just like the agent. Moreover, if the agent were not denoted, how could singularity be connected with it?

For it is not logical that a word should be connected with something that is not expressed by a word; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of [grammatical] operations such as *ūha*.
Furthermore, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*).

For it is not possible for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), which denotes only the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), to be coreferential with the word "Devadatta," because they do not reside in a single object. However, if [the suffix] denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), then coreferentiality is indeed established.
Furthermore, the contradiction with the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) stating "the suffix *la* [is used] in the sense of the agent" would be quite evident if the agent were not denoted.

Moreover, if the agent were not denoted, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "devadattena pacati" (Devadatta cooks by means of himself). For the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed for the agent and the instrument when they are not already denoted; since the agent would not be denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the third case ending expressing the agent would necessarily occur.

If, however, the agent is expressed [by a finite verb], the third case ending does not apply simply because it has already been expressed, since that [third case] falls under the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed"). On the other hand, the nominative (*prathamā*) certainly applies in the example "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), because the nominative is a case ending for a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) that has been expressed, or because it denotes merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor is the nominative redundant at that time, because its purpose is to convey gender and number, as the meaning of the stem alone has already been stated; furthermore, the use of a bare nominal stem is ungrammatical.
Furthermore, if the agent were not denoted by the verbal suffix, there would be the usage "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattena pacati*).
Therefore, it is established that the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix; such is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, they say:
For that alone is the meaning of a word which cannot be obtained by any other means; according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which is not obtainable otherwise.
For this very reason, the bank is not the primary meaning of the word *gaṅgā*, since its cognition is possible through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone.
And for this same reason, there is no expressive power (*śakti*) in a sentence-meaning.

Thus, since the *bhāvanā* expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is untenable without an agent, it implies that agent. Since the cognition of the agent can arise through this very implication (*ākṣepa*), why should the verbal suffix be postulated as its direct denoter? Furthermore, there is no decisive criterion [for such a postulation]. For the agent is one who possesses volitional effort (*kṛti*); and since it is possible for the *bhāvanā*—which is synonymous with volitional effort—to be the denotation of the verbal suffix according to the principle of the "Section on Form" (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*), one should not postulate that the possessor of that effort, the agent, is the denotation. This is because it would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor should it be said that the verbal suffix (*bhāvanā*), even though connected with other factors of action (*kāraka*), does not immediately imply the agent by abandoning them; for while it is necessarily connected with the agent, it is not so connected with other factors such as the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because in verbs such as "he stands" (*tiṣṭhati*), the suffix does not imply those [other factors].
Therefore, first of all, it implies the agent alone, and not any other factor of action.

For this very reason, the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is not connected with another *kāraka* (participant in the action), because that other participant is not present to the mind at first. For this same reason, the instrumental and other case-endings have as their primary denotation the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; for there is no necessary connection between the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) and those [participants], and thus they cannot be necessarily implied by it. Furthermore, even before hearing the verbal suffix, when the instrumental and other case-endings are heard, the cognition of the instrument and so forth arises.

Nor should it be asked how a number denoted by a word can be construed with an agent who is not denoted by a word; for we accept that the agent is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
Just as a bank indicated by a certain mark is followed by the word "sound," so too the agent, being thus indicated, will be understood as being one and the same.

For this very reason, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established in the expression "Devadatta cooks," because the agent is indicated [by the verbal suffix]. Nor should it be argued: "Since the primary meaning is possible, why should an indicated (metaphorical) sense be accepted? For it has been established that the meaning of a word must be something not obtainable through any other means.

Otherwise, even the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta is a lion" would have to be primary. Furthermore, even in the view of those who maintain that the agent (*kartṛ*) is denoted by the verb (*ākhyāta*), the co-referentiality in "Devadatta cooks" is not primary; for in their view, the verb denotes the factor of agency (*kāraka*) as an agent consisting of a mere power (*śakti*) abstracted [from its substrate], just like the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*). This is because the substance (*dravya*) possessing that power is not denoted, according to the principle of the *akṛtyadhikaraṇa*, while the word "Devadatta" denotes the substance alone.

Furthermore, because they are directed toward different objects, even in the case of the object (*karman*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not primary; rather, it is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). Thus, there is no distinction [between the two cases].

Nor should it be argued that the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) on the strength of the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) stating "the *L* affixes [denote] the agent" (*laḥ kartari*).

For the relationship between the signifier and the signified is not dependent upon grammatical tradition; rather, it is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) supported by reasoning (*nyāya*).
Or, let it be that this is accessible through traditional authority (*smṛti*).

Even so, this *smṛti* is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix; rather, it is an authoritative means of knowledge for the following point: that when there is oneness of the agent, the *lakāra* consists of the singular number; when there is duality, it consists of the dual number; and when there is plurality, it consists of the plural number—since this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with the rule: "The dual and singular endings are used for two and one respectively, and the plural ending for many.
As for what was said—that if the agent were not denoted, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the instrumental case in "Devadattena pacati" (Devadatta cooks)—that is not correct.

For the third [case-ending] is indeed intended for the purpose of expressing the agent (*kartṛ*) or for the purpose of expressing the number residing in that [agent]. In this regard, since the agent is obtained precisely through the implication (*ākṣepa*) of the verbal action (*bhāvanā*), there is no requirement for the third case there; and since its number is understood by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) itself, there is likewise no requirement for it there either.
As they have said:
"For the cognition of number or of the agent proceeds by means of a case-ending; and both of these are established here through the verbal suffix (*bhāvanā*) and the nominal suffix (*tan*).
However, where the number pertaining to that [agent] is not expressed by the verb, there the third case (*tṛtīyā*) certainly occurs."
As in the case of "Devadatta cooks rice";
since there is no fault whatsoever in not denoting the agent in that instance, enough with this excessive detail— let us proceed with the subject at hand.
Thus established, the application by means of direct statement (*śruti*) is threefold.
This *śruti* is the most powerful means of proof (*pramāṇa*) among [the six], such as indicative power (*liṅga*) and the rest;
for in the case of *liṅga* and the others, there is no directly perceived word that effects the application, but rather one must be inferred.

And as long as they [the other means] are postulating an indicative word (*liṅga*) for application, so long has the application already been effected by a directly perceived scriptural statement (*śruti*); thus, their power to effect such a postulation is frustrated, and therefore the scriptural statement possesses superior force. For this very reason, in the case of the text "With the *aindrī* [verse], he worships the *gārhapatya* [fire]," while the indicative power (*liṅga*) is still postulating that the *aindrī* verse is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the worship of Indra, the directly perceived scriptural statement establishes that it is a subordinate element for the worship of the *gārhapatya* fire; thus, the *aindrī* verse is a subordinate element for the worship of the *gārhapatya*. Indicative power (*liṅga*) is functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
As they say:
"The capacity of all things is designated as the *liṅga* (indicative mark).

By this, [the mantra] possesses the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*); just as, for example, the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" has the status of an auxiliary to the act of cutting.
For it is capable of making saltness manifest;

therefore, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is of two kinds: that which does not depend on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish the general relationship, and that which does depend upon it. Among these, when one thing is absolutely impossible without another, the former is subordinate to the latter by virtue of the indicative mark alone, independent of anything else.
Just as the knowledge of the meaning [of a mantra] is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) for the performance of the ritual action;

for indeed, the performance is not possible without the knowledge of the meaning. Whatever is possible without something else, that [latter thing] has the former as its purpose and depends upon it. For example, the aforementioned mantra is a subordinate factor for the act of cutting.
For indeed, cutting can be accomplished even without a mantra by means of other methods;

therefore, a mantra cannot have "cutting" as its own essential meaning. Rather, its purpose is to reveal the cutting that serves as a means for producing the *apūrva* (unseen spiritual potency). And this [specific] essence is not understood through mere capacity alone, because [the mantra] possesses the capacity merely to reveal the act of cutting.

Therefore, one must necessarily accept that context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth indicate a general relationship. For, since the mantra is recited within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is understood from its very placement there that "something related to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is manifested by this mantra"; otherwise, the recitation within the context would be rendered purposeless.

When the question arises as to what that thing related to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is which is to be manifested, it is understood by implication to be the "cutting of the *barhis* grass. For that [cutting] is related to the *apūrva* through the mediation of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *barhis*; thus, since the mantra serves that purpose by virtue of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*), the charge of meaninglessness does not apply.

Therefore, it is established that the mantra "I cut the *barhis*, the seat of the gods," having been understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) as being connected to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), is by its own capacity a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the cutting.

Regarding the mantras for the *anumantraṇa* (recitation after an act) dedicated to Pūṣan, once a general connection with sacrifice is understood through the designation (*samākhyā*) "sacrifice-recitation," their specific connection with the sacrifice to Pūṣan is understood by virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Now, it may be argued that while the general connection of those mantras with the sacrifice to Pūṣan is being understood through the designation, the general connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices themselves is already understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*), since context is more powerful than designation.

For this very reason, it has been stated that even though the *prayāja* offerings are mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa section titled "Instruction on Mantras," they are subsidiary to both the *sānnāyya* and *upāṃśuyāja* offerings due to the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, by the designation (*samākhyā*) "mantra for the consecration of the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantraṇa*), no specific connection with the *pūṣayāga* is understood; rather, there is only a general connection with "sacrifice" (*yāga*) in general. However, through the context (*prakaraṇa*), a specific connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) alone is understood.

Therefore, since the connection with that [deity] is immediately understood from the context, it is proper that those [mantras] have that very deity as their purpose; for the word *pūṣan*, through its etymological derivation from "he nourishes" (*puṣṇāti*), somehow denotes Agni and others as well. This is not so; for in the case of a mantra used for the consecration of Pūṣan, it is understood precisely as it is heard [in the text].

Because this mantra possesses the capacity to denote Pūṣan, it is for the purpose of manifesting him, just as the word "salt" is for the purpose of manifesting salt; in that case, there is no dependence on context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, by virtue of which those [other means] might possess greater force through being its basis of reliance.

However, since the context establishes that [the mantra] is dependent upon the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the context possesses greater force because it is the basis of reliance for the indicative power (*liṅga*), which in turn functions as the applicator by postulating the syntactical connection (*vākya*), the indicative power, and the direct statement (*śruti*).

From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), once it is understood that the purpose is to manifest Pūṣan, the manifestation of him alone would be purposeless; therefore, it must be stated that the purpose is to manifest Pūṣan as a means to the *apūrva*.

When the question arises, "What is that *apūrva*?", it is understood from the indicative mark—supported by the name (*sāmākhyā*) "Yāgānumantraṇa"—that this mantra is for the purpose of manifesting the deity connected with the *apūrva* of the sacrifice to Pūṣan.

Therefore, although *prakaraṇa* (context) is stronger than *sāmākhyā* (name/designation), nevertheless, because the former is sublated by *liṅga* (indicative power), it is the *sāmākhyā* itself that can serve as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the general connection; for even though weak, it possesses strength by relying upon a powerful *liṅga*, since even that which is weak gains strength when supported by something powerful.

For this very reason, although the Smṛti is weaker than Śruti, it possesses greater force because it is based on a primary ritual act (padārtha) in the form of sipping water (ācamana). Consequently, by abandoning the order prescribed by Śruti—which is a subordinate quality (guṇa) of the ritual act—one must perform the sipping of water immediately after the preparation of the Veda (vedakaraṇa), as has been stated.
As they say:
"Even the most powerful people among the city-dwellers and country-folk are overpowered by men who, though weak, have taken refuge with a king."
Thus [it is said].

As for the claim that the word *pūṣan* somehow denotes Agni and others, that is not so; for it is established by the remainder of the Vedic passage, such as "for he is toothless," and by Vedic usage, that the word has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) with respect to its specific referent; and conventional meaning is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*), which depends upon the consideration of the meanings of the word's constituent parts.

For this very reason, in the injunction "During the rains, the chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the sacred fires," the word *rathakāra* denotes a specific caste synonymous with the *saudhanvana*, because conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) prevails over etymological derivation (*yoga*). It does not refer to a member of the twice-born classes based on the etymology "one who makes a chariot" (*rathaṃ karoti*), because etymological derivation is weaker; as stated in the sixth book [of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra]. Therefore, it is logical that once a general connection is understood through the name (*samākhyā*), a specific connection with the sacrifice to Pūṣan arises for the mantras addressed to Pūṣan by virtue of their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*). As they say:

The designation "those which authorize the sacrifice" (*yāgānumantṛ*) serves as the factor that connects [the mantra] to the ritual (*kratu*); therefore, by virtue of its inherent capacity, its application occurs in a ritual dedicated to that same deity.

Thus it is established that *liṅga* (indicative power) is the factor that assigns a word-meaning whose general relationship [to the rite] is already established through other means of knowledge. In this regard, the *liṅga* that assigns a mantra applies it only to the primary meaning, not to the secondary one; for since the primary meaning presents itself first, once the cognition of application has reached its conclusion regarding that alone, to postulate an application again for the secondary meaning would result in the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that the mantra "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods" is, by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), an auxiliary to the cutting of *kuśa* grass because that is its primary meaning, and not an auxiliary to the cutting of *ulapa* grass.
This indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the other means of proof;
