Among these, "Having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*" is an injunction concerning mere sequence, because the making of the *vedi* and so forth have already been prescribed by another statement.

The statement "the first consumption belongs to the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*" refers to a ritual act qualified by its sequence; for it is impossible to enjoin mere sequence while restating the act of consumption, lest the integrity of the single syntactical unit (*ekaprasaratā*) be violated.

Furthermore, this direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than other means of proof, because those others possess the status of proof for sequence only by way of implying a verbal injunction (*vacana*).

For this very reason, although the cup for the Aśvins would have been taken in the third position according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), it is stated that it is taken in the tenth position based on the scriptural injunction: "The cup for the Aśvins is taken as the tenth."

However, where the determination [of order] is based on purpose (*prayojana*), that is "order by purpose" (*ārtha-krama*); as in the case of the *agnihotra* oblation and the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).
For here, since the gruel serves the purpose of the oblation, its cooking is performed first on account of that purpose.
And this [order] is stronger than the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭha-krama*).

For if one were to perform [the rites] according to the order of recitation (*pāṭha*), there would be a subversion of the established purposes and the performance would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

Indeed, there is no visible purpose for that which occurs immediately after the oblation (*homa*). The sequence of those sentences which convey the constituent elements of the rite (*padārtha*) is the "order of recitation" (*pāṭhakrama*);
and from that, the sequence of the constituent elements is adopted.

For in whatever order the sentences have been recited, in that very same order they produce the cognition of meaning when studied, because the objects denoted by the words are performed according to the cognition of meaning. And that recitation is of two kinds: the recitation of mantras and the recitation of the Brāhmaṇas.

In that regard, the order which is adopted for the *āgneya* and *āgniṣomīya* offerings based on the sequence of their respective *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses is the "order of the mantra-text" (*mantrapāṭha*). And this order of the mantra-text is more authoritative than the order of the *brāhmaṇa*-text. This is because, at the time of performance, the mantra-text is more intimately connected (*antarangatva*) than the *brāhmaṇa* statement. For the *brāhmaṇa* statement, having fulfilled its purpose by instructing "this is to be done in this manner" prior to the performance, does not function again at the time of the actual performance.
Furthermore, we shall explain that mantras have no other purpose than to cause one to remember the objects associated with their ritual application (*prayoga*).

Therefore, since the order of performance depends on the order of recollection, and the order of that recollection depends on the order of the mantras, the recitation of mantras is an internal factor compared to the other [the Brāhmaṇa], and is thus more powerful.

For this very reason, although the Brāhmaṇa text prescribes the performance of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice first and the Āgneya sacrifice later, the order is instead determined by the mantra text: the Āgneya is performed first and the Agniṣomīya later; thus it has been stated.
"One offers the *samidh* [oblation] of the *prayāja*s; one offers the *tanūnapāt* [oblation]"—the order derived from such injunctive sentences is the "order of the Brāhmaṇa text.

And although these Brāhmaṇa sentences have fulfilled their purpose by enjoining the matter, nevertheless, because there is no other means of reminding one of the *prayāja*s, they themselves are accepted as the reminders. Thus, it is logical that they produce the recollection of the matter in the very same order in which they were studied; therefore, their performance should follow that same order.
Thus, it is established that the sequence of the *prayāja* offerings follows the order of the *brāhmaṇa* recitation.

Now, one might object: why is it accepted that the *brāhmaṇa* sentences—which have already fulfilled their purpose by being injunctive—serve as reminders of matters connected to the performance (*prayoga-samaveta-artha*) in the case of the *prayājas*, when there exist *yājyā-mantras* (offering verses) that remind one of such matters, just as they do in the case of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices? Nor should it be argued that the *brāhmaṇa* sentence is accepted as a reminder of the ritual act (*karma-smāraka*) because those *mantras* serve only to remind one of the deity (*devatā-smāraka*); for if that were so, the same acceptance of the *brāhmaṇa* as a reminder of the ritual act would necessarily follow even in the case of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices.
If there were no such fault [in our position],
then the greater authority of the recitation of mantras over the recitation of Brāhmaṇas would not exist.

For the reason that the mantras possess greater authority is precisely that they serve to remind one of the objects associated with the ritual performance (*prayoga-samaveta-artha*), whereas the other (the Brāhmaṇa) does not so remind.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that the Brāhmaṇa passage serves as a reminder of the ritual action (*karma*), then— because the Brāhmaṇa passage is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) by virtue of reminding one of the primary act, whereas the Mantras are "external" (*bahiraṅga*) by virtue of reminding one of the subordinate deities— the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa would be more authoritative than the recitation of the Mantras. Consequently, this would contradict the fifth book’s section (the *pañcamikādhikaraṇa*),
wherein it is stated that because the Mantra-recitation is more authoritative than the Brāhmaṇa-recitation, the *Āgneya* sacrifice is performed first and the *Agniṣomīya* sacrifice follows.

If it is argued that in the case of the *āgneya* and other offerings, it is the *yājyā* mantras themselves that reveal the ritual action by way of revealing the deity—since the nature of a deity consists in being the intended recipient of the substance being relinquished—then the same applies to the *prayāja* offerings.

For there too, the *yājyā* mantras reveal the deities, because in the *prayājas*, the deity is indicated by the wording of the mantra. Thus, since the *yājyā* mantras in the *prayājas* reveal the ritual action by way of revealing the deity, their sequence must be determined solely by the order of the mantra-text and not by the order of the *brāhmaṇa* text.
Nor should it be argued that because the recitation of the mantras is of a different nature, the order of the *prayāja* offerings follows the order of the *brāhmaṇa* text alone;
for if it were of a different nature, the performance would have to follow that very [mantra] order, since the order of the mantras is more authoritative.

Furthermore, in the *Abhiyāsa-adhikaraṇa*, the author of the Vārttika stated the sequential application of the *yājyā* mantras among the *prayājas* with the words: "In the case of the mantra-texts of the subsidiaries applied according to their sequence," and so forth.

In the ninth *Tantraratna*, it is stated that in passages such as "O Agni, [they] consume the fuel-sticks, the fuel-sticks, and the clarified butter," the deities are presented as subordinate factors (*guṇa*) by means of mantras obtained through the sequence and context;
if the mantras were arranged in a different order, this would be untenable.
If it is asked: "How then is there a sequence among the *prayāja* offerings based on the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa text?"—
It is said: This is true;

nevertheless, in cases where there are no mantras at all that remind one of the ritual acts—such as in rites performed in silence—their sequence is determined by the order of the Brāhmaṇa text, because it is those [Brāhmaṇa passages] alone that remind one of the matters connected with the performance.

The example of the *prayāja* offerings is given as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*), because in that case, the Brāhmaṇa sentences themselves lack the capacity to remind one of matters connected with the performance. As the authors of the Vārttika state in the section on Arthavādas: "In the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, the Ṛgvedic verses, having fulfilled their purpose by conveying the meaning, do not attain the status of being employed [as part of the ritual], even though they come into contact with the actual form [of the rite]."

Therefore, for rites accompanied by mantras, the sequence is determined by the order of the recitation of the mantras; however, for rites without mantras, the sequence is indeed from the order of the recitation of the Brāhmaṇa texts—this is the general principle.

In the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), when items located in various places must be performed at a single location in the ectype (*vikṛti*) due to a specific injunction, that item which is performed in its own place is performed first, and the other two follow afterward. This sequence is called the "sequence of position" (*sthānakrama*).
"Position" (*sthāna*) means "proximity" (*upasthiti*).
For when a rite is performed in a particular location, that very item which was performed immediately prior to it becomes the first to be present; thus, its performance first is logical.

For this very reason, in the Sādyaska sacrifice, although the Agniṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anubandhya animals are to be performed together at the location of the Savanīya, the performance of the Savanīya animal comes first. This is because, at that location, immediately after the drawing of the Āśvina cup, the Savanīya alone is the first to be present, while the other two follow later.
For instance, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are three animal sacrifices: the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Ānubandhya.
And these occupy different locations:
the Agniṣomīya on the day of preparation (aupavasathya), the Savanīya at the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā), and the Ānubandhya at the conclusion.
The *sādyaskra* is a specific type of Soma sacrifice;

because it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, those three animal sacrifices are also extended to the *sādyaskra* by means of the *atideśa* (extended application) of its archetypal rules.

And their conjunction (*sāhitya*) there is heard in the injunction: "One should immolate the animals together. That conjunction takes place at the location of the *savanīya* animal, because of its proximity to the primary sacrifice and because of the equality in the displacement from their respective positions.

For if the performance were carried out at the location of the *savanīya*, there would be merely a displacement from their own positions for both the *agniṣomīya* and the *ānubandhya*; whereas if the performance were carried out at the location of the *agniṣomīya*, there would be merely a displacement from its own position for the *savanīya*. However, for the *ānubandhya*, there would result both a displacement from its own position and a displacement from the position of the *savanīya*.

In this same manner, the [order] for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice should be understood at the location of the Ānubandhya sacrifice. Likewise, when the performance of all [the animal sacrifices] is to take place at the location of the Savanīya, the performance of the Savanīya must come first.

For the location of the Savanīya is immediately after the drawing of the Āśvina cup. In the archetype (prakṛti), having drawn the Āśvina cup and having thrice encircled the sacrificial post, one dedicates the Agneya Savanīya animal;
this is because its performance is prescribed immediately after the drawing of the Āśvina cup.

And likewise, in the Sādyaskra sacrifice as well, once the Āśvina cup has been drawn, the Savanīya offering alone becomes present; thus it is logical that its performance occurs first by virtue of its position, while the other two follow later—this is what was stated.
The order of subsidiaries that is adopted according to the order of the primary acts is called "order of the principal" (mukhyakrama).

For if the subsidiaries (aṅga) are performed in the very same order in which the principal acts (pradhāna) are performed, then all the subsidiaries maintain an equal distance from their respective principals; however, if they were performed out of that order, some subsidiaries would be entirely proximate to their principals while others would be excessively remote. That is improper, as it would result in the contraction of the interpretation, inconsistency, and the subversion of the primary meaning. Therefore, the order of the principals is also a cause for the order of the subsidiaries.

For this very reason, the sprinkling of the *āgneya* oblation occurs first with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings, and afterwards that of the *aindra* curds; because of the sequential order between the *āgneya* sacrifice and the *aindra* sacrifice. For here, each of the two sprinklings has an equal interval of one intervening element from its respective principal rite: because the sprinkling of the *āgneya* oblation is separated from the *āgneya* sacrifice by the sprinkling of the *aindra* sacrificial material; and because the sprinkling of the *aindra* sacrificial material is separated from the *aindra* sacrifice by the *āgneya* sacrifice.

Therefore, by virtue of the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*), the sequence is established as follows: first the sprinkling of the oblation for Agni, then that of the oblation for Indra, then the sacrifice to Agni, and finally the sacrifice to Indra.

However, if the sprinkling of the oblation for Indra were performed first and that of the oblation for Agni second, then—because the performance of the sacrifice to Agni would occur first due to the order of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—there would result an absolute lack of separation between the sacrifice to Agni and the sprinkling of its own oblation, while there would be an absolute separation between the sacrifice to Indra and the sprinkling of its own oblation.
And that is not tenable; therefore, it is logical that the sequence for the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* oblations follows the sequence of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*).
Furthermore, this *mukhyakrama* is weaker than the sequence of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

For *mukhyakrama* involves a delayed comprehension, as it depends upon the comprehension of the sequence of the principal acts, which itself depends on other means of knowledge. *Pāṭhakrama*, however, is stronger because it depends solely on the sequence of the textual recitation of the Veda, which is independent [of other factors].

For this very reason, although the *āgneya*, *upāṃśuyāja*, and *āgnīṣomīya* offerings are performed in their sequential order, the pouring out of the clarified butter for the *upāṃśuyāja* is not performed before [the pouring out for the *āgneya*], because that [sequential order] is weak. Rather, it is performed afterwards according to the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), because that is stronger. Furthermore, this order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger than the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*). For if the order of performance were adopted, there would be a great separation of many subordinate elements from their primary acts; whereas if this [order of the principal acts] is adopted, there is proximity.
For example:
at the beginning of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), there is first the performance of the Āgneya offering, and then that of the Sāṃnāyya;
furthermore, certain of its ritual requirements (dharmas) are performed beforehand.

In that case, if one were to follow the order of performance (*pravṛttikrama*) and first perform all the properties (*dharma*) of that [Sāṃnāyya], then the properties of the Āgneya, then the performance of the Āgneya, and finally the performance of the Sāṃnāyya, then there would be a separation (*viprakarṣa*) of those properties from their own primary rites by two steps: namely, by the properties of the Āgneya and its subsequent performance.

But when some of the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* are performed first, while all the others are performed subsequently by following the order of the primary acts (*mukhyakrama*), immediately after the performance of the properties of the *āgneya*, then there occurs for all the properties of the *āgneya* and the *sāṃnāyya* an intervention by a single item of a different class; because the properties of the *āgneya* are separated from their own primary act by the properties of the *sāṃnāyya*, and the properties of the *sāṃnāyya* are separated from their own primary act by the performance of the *āgneya*. Thus, there is no excessive distance (*viprakarṣa*).
Therefore, the order of primary performance (*pravṛttikrama*) is stronger than the order of principal acts (*mukhyakrama*).

When several principal acts are performed together, and the constituent parts (*aṅga*) that are to be performed in conjunction with them must be executed repeatedly, the sequence of the second and subsequent items according to the sequence of the first item already performed is called the order of primary performance. This is as seen in the case of the subsidiaries of the *prājāpatya* offerings.

For it is said: "Having performed the *vaiśvadevī*, they proceed with the *prājāpatyas*. Because of the indication by the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*), these [offerings] are to be performed simultaneously along with their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
Therefore, the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of those [Prājāpatya offerings] and the subsequent rites, such as the *upākaraṇa* and *niyojana*, must be accomplished.
In that regard, since the Prājāpatya offerings have a common deity, their concomitance is possible because they are performed at one and the same time;
however, it is impossible for their constituent parts (*aṅga*) to be performed at one and the same time.

For it is not possible to perform the ritual dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of many animals at one and the same time; therefore, their simultaneity must be achieved by performing them without interruption—that is, having performed the dedication of one, one performs the dedication of another. Consequently, among the *prājāpatya* offerings, after performing one ritual act (*padārtha*) everywhere, the second ritual act is to be performed.

In that context, the performance of the first ritual act (padārtha) must be commenced with a certain animal; however, the second ritual act must be performed in the very same sequence as the first was performed. This is for the sake of establishing the mutual concomitance (sāhitya) of the subsidiaries as understood from the injunction of performance (prayogavidhi).

For by the injunction of performance, the mutual concomitance—otherwise known as immediate succession—of the subsidiaries of the consecration rite (*daikṣa*), such as the bringing near (*upākaraṇa*) and the tying (*niyojana*), is prescribed.

And that *sāhitya* (simultaneity) is obtained for the *savanīya-paśu* by means of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), because it has a living creature as its substance and is thus a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *daikṣa* (initiation sacrifice).

It is obtained from the *savanīya* for the *ekādaśina* sacrifices due to their sharing the same time of the *sutyā*; and from those, it is obtained for the *prājāpatya* sacrifices according to the principle of the "thinness" (*tanutva*) of the connection.
Furthermore, regarding the *prājāpatya* sacrifices, since there is a distinct sacrifice for each animal, the *codakas* differ accordingly.

Therefore, by virtue of the *codaka* (extended injunction), the simultaneity—otherwise known as immediate succession—of the various subsidiary acts belonging to each animal, such as the ritual touching (*upākaraṇa*) and the tethering (*niyojana*), is established.
Consequently, it would follow that by the force of the *codaka*, the tethering must be performed immediately after the ritual touching of a single animal.
However, this is not done, because it is impossible to maintain the simultaneity of all subsidiary acts for every animal as understood from the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*).
Therefore, when the *upākaraṇa* (dedication) has been performed for one animal, even though *niyojana* (binding) would logically follow immediately thereafter, it is not performed.
However, by the force of an explicit scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣavacana*), the *upākaraṇa* alone is performed for the other sixteen animals.

Once the *upākaraṇa* has been performed for them, since there is no authority for delaying the *niyojana* of the first animal until after its own *upākaraṇa*, the *niyojana* must be performed on the first animal itself.
Therefore, the dedication (*niyojana*) must be performed in the very same order as the immolation (*upākaraṇa*) was performed.
In this way, each respective immolation of the animals maintains an equal interval of sixteen moments from its own dedication.
Otherwise, some would have an excessive interval, while others would have no interval at all.
And that is not logical.
Therefore, by whatever sequence the first ritual act was performed, by that very same sequence the second must be performed.
Thus it is established that the sequence of the second ritual act which follows from the sequence of the first performed act is called the *pravṛttikrama* (the order of performance).
Thus, the operation of the injunction regarding the ritual procedure (*prayogavidhi*) has been briefly defined by means of the sixfold classification.
An injunction that makes known the ownership of the fruit (*phalasvāmya*) is an injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*).
And the ownership of the fruit consists in being the enjoyer of the result produced by the ritual action.
And that [injunction] is of such a form as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice.
For, by prescribing the sacrifice with reference to heaven, it establishes that the one who desires heaven is the enjoyer of the fruit produced by the sacrifice.

However, by injunctions such as "he whose fire-altar has been established and whose house is burned by fire should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kṣāmavat," which prescribe an action when a specific occasion like the burning of a house occurs, it is established that the one possessing the occasion (the *nimittavat*) has ownership of the fruit in the form of the removal of sin (*pakṣaya*) produced by the ritual act.
And that ownership of the fruit belongs only to him who is distinguished by the specific qualification of the person entitled [to the rite].
And that alone is the qualification of the person entitled which is heard as a qualification of the person.

For this very reason, although the injunction "A king desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" prescribes the Rājasūya with reference to sovereignty, it does not establish that the status of being the enjoyer of that fruit belongs to anyone merely desiring sovereignty; rather, it belongs to one who is already a king and desires it.

However, even if it is not explicitly heard as a qualification of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*), it may nonetheless be a qualification of the qualified agent (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*); for example, the knowledge established by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the possession of fire established by the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) in rites accomplished by means of fire, and [physical] capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Even though these [attributes] are not heard as qualifications of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*), they certainly exist as qualifications of the qualified performer (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*); for the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices proceed only toward one who possesses knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study, since those injunctions lack the power to project the requirement of knowledge. And since rites to be accomplished by means of the sacred fires depend upon those fires, their injunctions proceed only toward one who possesses the fires established by the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). For this very reason, a Śūdra has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to sacrifice and the like, because he lacks the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study and the fires established by the rite of fire-consecration.

Since the qualification for Vedic study (*adhyayana*) belongs to those who have undergone initiation (*upanīta*), and since initiation itself—according to such injunctions as "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age"—is restricted to the three *varṇas*; and although the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is prescribed for the *rathakāra* (the chariot-maker, also known by the synonym *saudhanvana*) by the rule "during the rainy season, the *rathakāra* should establish the fire"—for etymological derivation (*yoga*) is stronger than conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—nevertheless, he has no qualification for the subsequent rites (*uttara-karma*), because he lacks the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study.

Nor should it be argued that since that [knowledge] is absent even when the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) is performed, how can there be entitlement to its performance, given that it is accomplished by that [knowledge]? For even in the absence of knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study, this very injunction—"In the rainy season, the *rathakāra* shall consecrate the fires"—implies the knowledge necessary merely for the consecration; otherwise, that very injunction would be untenable.
Consequently, although the *rathakāra* has entitlement to the mere consecration, he lacks entitlement to the subsequent rites due to the absence of [general] learning (*vidyā*).

And thus, that establishment [of the fires] is not for the purpose of consecrating the fires, because there is no further utility for the consecrated fires later on. Rather, that establishment—possessing the quality of a worldly fire—is prescribed as an independent primary ritual act (*pradhānakarma*) with heaven as its fruit, according to the logic of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the accusative case in the word "fires" (*agnīn*) is used in the sense of the instrumental, as in the expression "he offers the powers" (*śaktīr juhoti*).
Let us now return to the subject at hand.

Thus it is established that because a Śūdra lacks the knowledge acquired through the injunction for Vedic study and lacks the fires established by the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), he has no entitlement to the subsequent ritual acts. If it is argued: "In that case, a woman would likewise have no entitlement, since she lacks the knowledge established by that injunction due to the prohibition against her Vedic study; nor can it be said that she has no entitlement at all, because in such injunctions as 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice' (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), the word 'desirer of heaven' serves to present the person qualified for the act (*uddeśya*). Since masculinity is not an intended qualification of the qualified person—just like the singularity of the cup (*graha*)—it has been established that a woman does indeed have entitlement. [Response: This is not so. For the Śūdra, even the mere knowledge of the meaning of the texts is impossible, as he is excluded from the study of the Vedas. however, the qualification [of the wife] has been established as subordinate (*adhikāra*), not independently (*svātantryeṇa*). Therefore, since husband and wife possess joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*), the wife’s accomplishment of the ritual purpose is achieved through the knowledge of the sacrificer alone; thus, there is no logical inconsistency in her entitlement even without [independent] knowledge. This is analogous to the case of the *niṣādasthapati*. Although he lacks the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study, his entitlement is determined by the statement: "One should cause this *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice with this [offering]. For in the compound *niṣādasthapati*, it is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "a chief (stapati) who is a Niṣāda," and not a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* meaning "the chief of the Niṣādas. This is because the latter interpretation would necessitate a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the sense of the genitive case.
However, there is this distinction:

because the Niṣāda lacks the knowledge established by the injunction for Vedic study, it is precisely this [present] injunction that necessitates the knowledge required for his specific ritual action.

As for the wife, although she lacks such knowledge, she has the right to participate together with the sacrificer; and since he possesses such knowledge and the accomplishment of her duty is achieved through him alone, the subsequent injunctions regarding the ritual acts do not necessitate her own knowledge.

However, those ritual acts performed solely by the wife, such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*) and so forth, cannot be performed by one who lacks knowledge—being like a "fist of a non-agent. Therefore, it is accepted that the injunctions for those acts imply the acquisition of such knowledge. Thus, it is established that both the knowledge acquired through the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) and the possession of wealth established by the injunction for setting up the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) serve as qualifications for the subsequent rites. In this same way, capacity (*sāmarthya*) is also a qualification for eligibility, because an injunction does not apply to one who is incapable, according to the maxim: "For verbal roots expressing an action, capacity is a necessary concomitant."

And that capacity, in the case of an optional (*kāmya*) rite, pertains to both the subsidiaries and the principal act; however, one who is incapable of the subsidiaries but capable of the principal act alone is not entitled (*adhikārī*) to the optional rite. This is because the injunction for the principal act, having attained syntactic unity with the injunctions for the subsidiaries, operates only with respect to one capable of performing the rite together with its subsidiaries, since entitlement follows the application of the injunctions as they are prescribed. For if it were the case that the injunction operated only toward one who is capable, yet there were a contradiction with some scriptural text (*śruti*), then even one who is incapable would have entitlement. But such is not the case.

And there is no contradiction; for the injunction regarding one who desires heaven (*svargakāmaśruti*) functions only with respect to a capable person, and thus there is no contradiction. On the contrary, if it were to function with respect to an incapable person, there would result the sublation of the requirement of the combination of subsidiaries (*aṅgasāhitya*), which is understood through the syntactic unity of the subsidiary injunctions with the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*). Furthermore, this would entail the contingency that the subsidiaries, which are heard as being obligatory (*nityavat*), become merely optional. Therefore, eligibility for a ritual performed for a specific desire (*kāmyakarman*) belongs only to one who is capable of performing it along with its subsidiaries.
However, in the case of obligatory rituals (*nityakarman*), the principle of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) applies to the subsidiaries.
For these [obligatory rites] are enjoined by the scriptural injunction "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva*) as duties to be performed for the duration of one's life.

Yet, it is not possible for anyone to perform the ritual application (*prayoga*) with all its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*) for the entire span of life. Therefore, regarding obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), the qualified performer (*adhikārī*) is one capable of performing at least the principal act (*pradhāna*); however, as many auxiliaries as can be performed, those many should be carried out. Let us stop this prolixity, as the learned masters have already exerted great effort on this point.
Thus it is established that an injunction which makes known one's ownership of the fruit is an *adhikāra-vidhi* (injunction of qualification).
In this way, by defining its fourfold division, it has been demonstrated that an injunction culminates in a purposeful meaning.
Furthermore, mantras possess utility by virtue of reminding one of the objects associated with the performance of the ritual action.

However, that utterance is not for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), because when a visible purpose is possible, it is improper to assume an unseen one. Nor is the recitation of mantras useless, since the visible purpose is possible through other means as well; this is because one resorts to a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that "it must be remembered by means of mantras alone. A restrictive injunction is an injunction that applies when two means are available as options, but which prescribes one of those means at a time when that specific means would otherwise not have been obtained.
As they have said:

"An injunction (*vidhi*) applies when [an action] is not established at all; a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applies when it is optionally established; and an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) is proclaimed when it is established both there and elsewhere."
This is its meaning:

an *apūrva-vidhi* (injunction of what was not previously established) is an injunction that prescribes for something a purpose that has not been obtained through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*), and so forth.
For the fact that the sacrifice has heaven as its purpose is not established by any other means of knowledge prior to this very injunction; therefore, this is an *apūrva-vidhi*.
However, a rule that prescribes what has not been obtained as an alternative is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), such as "One threshes the rice grains" and so forth.

For by this injunction, the fact that threshing serves the purpose of removing the husk is not being made known, since that is already established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); rather, it is a restriction.

And that [completion] consists in the fulfillment of the unobtained portion (*aprāptāṃśapūraṇa*). For since threshing (*avaghāta*) can be accomplished by various means, there is a state in which one begins to adopt another means while setting aside threshing. In that state, because threshing is unobtained, this injunction performs the very fulfillment of the unobtained portion, consisting in the prescription of that [threshing]. Therefore, in a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), the meaning of the sentence is precisely the restriction itself, consisting in the fulfillment of the unobtained portion; that is to say, it is the prescription of threshing at the time when it is unobtained as an alternative. It is not, however, a prescription based on absolute non-obtention, as is the case with an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

When two options are simultaneously applicable, an injunction whose purpose is the exclusion of the other is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*); for example, "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. This sentence is not intended as an injunction to eat, because eating [meat] is already established through natural desire (*rāga*). Nor is it intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because since the eating of both five-nailed and non-five-nailed animals is simultaneously applicable, there is no possibility of its non-application in any particular case. Therefore, this is intended to exclude the eating of five-nailed animals other than those five; thus, it is a restrictive injunction. And that restriction is of two kinds: scriptural (*śrauti*) and indicatory (*lākṣaṇikī*).

In this context, the restriction "for they pour [the cups] here indeed" (tatrā 'tra hy evā 'vapanti) is scriptural (śrauti), because the word "indeed" (eva) expresses the exclusion of the stotras other than the Pavamāna.
However, in the case of "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," the restriction is figurative (lākṣaṇikī), because there is no word expressing the exclusion of others.
For this very reason, the latter is afflicted by the three defects.
And there are three defects: the abandonment of what is heard (*śrutahāni*), the postulation of what is not heard (*aśrutakalpanā*), and the sublation of what is established (*prāptabādha*).

[These follow] from abandoning what is heard—the eating of five-clawed animals—postulating the cessation of eating five-clawed animals other than those five which is not heard, and sublating the eating of five-clawed animals other than those five which is already established. Among these three defects, two reside in the word (*śabda*), while the defect of sublation resides in the meaning (*artha*); such is the general direction [of the argument].
Since it is established that [the mantra] must be remembered by means of the mantras themselves—by resorting to this restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi)—the mantras are not meaningless.

Consequently, it is logical that the mantras possess purposefulness by way of reminding one of the matters connected with the performance. In that regard, if those mantras which are recited in a particular place can serve the purpose of illuminating the meaning there, then their application (viniyoga) is precisely in that place.
However, for those [formulas] for which [the primary purpose] is not possible, their excellence (*utkarṣa*) occurs wherever such possibility exists,

as has been stated regarding the *pūṣānumantraṇa* and *mantra*s. But for those [formulas] for which [the primary purpose] is not possible anywhere, the recitation of them must, out of necessity, have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*).

In every respect, however, those names are not meaningless; they possess purposefulness by way of delimiting the meaning of the enjoined object. For instance, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the word *udbhid* is the name of a sacrifice.
And by that [injunction], the determination of the object to be performed is effected.
For, since it has not been previously established, this sentence enjoins a sacrifice with reference to a result;
and since a sacrifice in its general form cannot be enjoined, it is specifically a particular sacrifice that is enjoined.

In response to the inquiry, "What is that distinction [implied] there?", it is understood from the word *udbhid* that the sacrifice is of the nature of *udbhid*, because of the connection of the name through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as in "by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice. Furthermore, its coreferentiality with the sacrifice is not like that of words such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). For in that case, the denoted object of the word "blue" is the quality of blueness, which is distinct from the lotus—the referent of the word "lotus."
All of that [the sacrifice] stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [the word "udbhid"].

However, for the word *udbhid*, there is no denoted meaning other than a specific sacrifice found among its synonyms, because it denotes a particular [sacrifice]. Consequently, since it does not denote a different object, the name does not stand in coreferentiality like the word "blue" (*nīla*); rather, it is like the word "curd-mixture" (*āmikṣā*) in the expression "the curd-mixture for the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevyāmikṣā*).

For the word *vaiśvadevī* ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix denoting a deity; and since it is recorded that such a suffix occurs in the sense of "this is its deity" (*sā asya devatā*), which is the referent of a pronoun, pronouns denote a specific [entity] by virtue of expressing what is proximate. When the expectation arises as to what specific entity is conveyed by the word *vaiśvadevī*, it is understood—due to the proximity of the word *āmikṣā*—that the specific entity is the form of *āmikṣā*.
As they say:

"This secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) indeed expresses *āmikṣā* as being connected with a deity; due to its proximity to the word *āmikṣā*, it merely presents that very [substance] as the object [of the deity].
Thus it is said.
Likewise:

"The meaning of the subordinate term (*upapada*) is denoted by the pronoun through direct audition (*śruti*); its meaning [in turn] is denoted by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Thus, there is a single denotation for these three.

Therefore, just as the word *āmikṣā* stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *vaiśvadevī* by virtue of providing the specific [substance] conveyed by the word *vaiśvadevī*, so too, since a general [term] cannot be that which is enjoined, the name stands in coreferentiality with the sacrifice understood from the *yājyā* verse by virtue of providing the specific sacrifice.
Thus it is established that names possess purposefulness by means of delimiting the meaning of the injunction;
as they say:
"Because the accomplishment of the specific sacrifice depends upon that. And the status of being a name arises from four causes.

[This is established] for fear of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), for fear of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because there is no scriptural injunction regarding that [name] as a primary element, and because of its designation as such. In this regard, in the passage "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the word *udbhid* is the name of a sacrifice for fear of a possessive indication. If the word *udbhid* were to convey a quality (*guṇa*), then it would not be appropriate to enjoin that quality by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice, because this would result in the fruit-word becoming meaningless.
Nor is it possible for this sentence to enjoin the sacrifice with respect to the fruit while simultaneously enjoining a proximate quality, as that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Nor is it possible for there to be an injunction of a connection between a quality and a result, because that would entail the injunction of a remote matter by means of enjoining a different primary category (padārtha). Furthermore, since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is neither enjoined in its own form nor is anything else enjoined with reference to it, the verbal root would result in being entirely subservient to another (atyantapārārthya), and the *yājyā* mantra would likewise become purposeless. For in that case, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not presented by this [injunction], because the quality is construed as the instrument; nor is the result presented, because the animal (*paśu*) is construed as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*).

Now, if it is argued that in the injunction establishing the relationship between the quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit (*phala*), the sacrifice (*yāga*) is connected as the substratum (*āśraya*), we say no; for in the expression "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is no word denoting the state of being a substratum.
If it is further argued that, just as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is indicated (*lakṣya*) in the final view (*siddhānta*), so too is the state of being a substratum indicated, we say no.
Since instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is simpler than substratumhood (*āśrayatva*), it is more appropriate to define [the sacrifice] by that [instrumentality].

That in which a quality (*guṇa*) being enjoined for the sake of a result attains the status of a causal factor (*kāraka*) is the substratum (*āśraya*). And its nature is indeed substratumhood; whereas instrumentality is an abstracted power (*śakti*), and thus there is simplicity. Furthermore, when the connection between a quality and a result is enjoined, the quality—having become an instrument—or the instrumentality residing therein, must be enjoined with reference to the result.

In that regard, in the first alternative, since the instrumentality (karaṇatva) is subordinate to the quality (guṇa), its cognition must be stated as being due to indication (lakṣaṇā) alone; for instrumentality is the meaning of the instrumental suffix (tṛtīyā-pratyaya), and it is logically appropriate for it to be primary.

Even when the instrumentality residing in the quality is to be enjoined with reference to the result, even then the presentation of the instrumentality residing in the quality—which is fit for syntactic connection (anvaya) with the efficient-force directed toward the result (phala-bhāvanā)—must be stated as being due to indication alone; because the factor of instrumentality expressed by the instrumental case, while fit for connection with the action, is unfit for connection [with the result] as an instrument.

For the instrumental factor (*kāraka*) denoted by the word "instrument" (*karaṇa-śabda*) is unfit for syntactic connection as such [an instrument], not that which is denoted by the third case suffix (*tṛtīyā*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a further third case suffix arising after a third case suffix, just as it arises after the word "instrument.

Therefore, the presentation of the instrument-status residing in a quality—which is fit for connection as an instrument—must be understood as being expressed solely through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, the instrumentality belonging to a quality—which is either presented through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as being instrumental or has already become instrumental—within the productive activity toward the fruit (*phalabhāvanā*), must also be expressed by secondary indication alone. This is because the heard instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the instrumentality of the quality alone with respect to the sacrifice.

For this very reason, it is stated that the status of the *godohana* vessel and so forth as being for the sake of cattle arises from their syntactic connection (*samabhivyāhāra*), since they have become instruments in the act of fetching water for the jar (*ghaṭabhramaṇe*).

Therefore, since enjoining a connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*) would entail numerous defects—such as the verbal root (*dhātu*) being entirely subservient to another meaning—it must be accepted that the injunction is simply for an action qualified by a quality, provided that the word *udbhid* conveys that quality.

For in that case, the root *yaj* indicates only the instrument (*karaṇatva*), which is a minimal requirement, and the stem portion of the word *udbhid* indicates only the possessive sense (*matvartha*). Thus, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) compared to enjoining a connection between a quality and a fruit.

However, it is simply not the case that the verbal root (*dhātu*) possesses such qualities as being entirely subservient to another; rather, it is the meaning of the root itself that is indicated (*lakṣaṇā*) with reference to the result.

Consequently, if the word *udbhid* were to convey a quality (*guṇa*), one would have to accept the injunction of a ritual action qualified by that quality, having first indicated a possessive sense (*matvartha*) through it—namely, "one should effect the attainment of cattle by means of a sacrifice characterized by *udbhid-ness*.

But if it is a name of the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), there is no indication of a possessive sense for the word *udbhid*, because its connection is possible through its primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*) in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice): "one should effect the attainment of cattle by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice."
Furthermore, it is not proper to resort to secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) when the primary meaning is possible;
moreover, the proximity of the injunction remains exactly the same.

Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, the word *soma* in the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*) would also result in being the name of a sacrifice, because if it were to convey a quality (guṇa), it would entail the fault of indicating a possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). This is because the word *soma* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that [botanical] sense, and thus it cannot logically be the name of a sacrifice; rather, one must resort to secondary indication only as a last resort.

However, no such well-known meaning is established for the word *udbhid*; for the etymological derivation (*yoga*)—namely, "that by which one breaks forth" (*udbhidyate 'nena*)—is applicable to the sacrifice as well, just as it is to a quality, since the sacrifice brings about the breaking forth of the fruit.
Thus it is established that the word *udbhid* functions as the name of a sacrifice (*yāganāmadheya*) out of fear of implying a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

In the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*," the word *citrayā* functions as the name of a ritual action (*karmānāmadheya*) out of fear of resulting in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
For instance:

first of all, the injunction of a sacrifice qualified by an accessory (guṇa) is not possible here. Since the sacrifice has already been enjoined by the statement, "Curd, honey, milk, ghee, parched grain, water, and rice—these mixed together are for Prajāpati," it is impossible to enjoin that same sacrifice as qualified [by another accessory]. Furthermore, if both the connection of that sacrifice with a result and its connection with an accessory were to be enjoined simultaneously, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

Now, since from the word *citrā* there arises the cognition of both variegatedness (*citratva*) and feminity (*stritva*), and since feminity by its very nature is a property of living beings (*prāṇidharma*), it is impossible for it to apply to the ritual action under discussion which consists of substances such as curd; therefore, by this sentence, there is no injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) regarding the ritual action at hand, but rather regarding a ritual action involving a living being as the substance.

In this regard, because this sentence is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), and because of the principle that "independent injunctions apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) unless there is a redundancy," it pertains to the archetype. Furthermore, since sacrifices whose substance is a living being have the *agniṣomīya* sacrifice as their archetype—according to the principle that "the *daikṣa* [initiation] applies to the others"—a quality is prescribed by this sentence with reference to that [archetype].

Furthermore, since the *dīkṣā* (initiatory rite) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma and thus lacks any expectation for an independent fruit, the term "animal sacrifice" (*paśubandha*) does not refer to a separate result; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the desire already established as an auxiliary to the production of the animal through the *unmīya* rite.

If it is argued that, in this way, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), even so, there is indeed a syntactical split characterized by prolixity (*gaurava*), whether one posits the injunction of "variegatedness" (*citratva*) and "femininity" (*stritva*) by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the animal of the *dīkṣā* sacrifice, or the injunction of a qualified factor (*viśiṣṭakāraka*). This is because the factor itself is already established [by other means], making a qualified injunction untenable; and furthermore, since the word "desire" (*kāma*) naturally refers to a result, treating it as a mere restatement of desire would lead to its meaninglessness (*ānarthakyāpatti*). Moreover, the desire to acquire an animal does not necessarily exist [prior to the act], as such a desire is absent when an animal has already been given by someone prior to the desire itself.

And thus, the establishment [of the injunction] follows from the fact that the term "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) is heard as a constant [requirement]. Furthermore, because the animal for the *daikṣa* sacrifice is already restricted by the masculinity prescribed in its originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), it is impossible to enjoin femininity therein—just as it is impossible to enjoin whey (*vājina*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice. Moreover, since the animal is already restricted by the specific color of the black-spotted deer (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*) prescribed in its own immediate context—as in the rule "the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma is black-spotted"—it is impossible to enjoin variegatedness (*citra*) through a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) taught independently (*anārabhya-adhīta*), just as it is impossible to enjoin the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*) when the number fifteen (*pañcadaśya*) has already been established.

Now, let it not be that there is an injunction of variegatedness (*citratva*) and femininity (*stritva*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; rather, let there be an injunction of qualities by way of a reference to the ewe prescribed as a subsidiary of the sacrifice in the sentence "a ewe for Sarasvatī" (*sārasvatī meṣī*). This is because, in the word *citrayā*, there is an injunction of variegatedness with respect to the feminine grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

Nor should it be argued that an injunction of variegatedness is improper because the requirement is satisfied by the natural black-spotted color (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga-varṇa*); for it is possible for the enjoined variegatedness to sublate the other color that is extended [from the archetype] by implication (*atideśa*). If this is your position—

For it is not possible for the mention of the feminine agent (*strī-kāraka*) and the prescription of "variegatedness" (*citratva*) to occur by means of the single word *citrayā*; this is because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), characterized by the violation of the principle of "single-sweep" (*ekaprasaratā*), since the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) must be established through multiple words.

For this very reason, it was stated in the third [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras] that in the case of the rule *vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ* ("The first draught belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call"), there is a prescription of a qualified drinking, and not a prescription of priority (*prāthamya*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the act of drinking.

Furthermore, if one were to determine that the goat (*meṣī*) is the subject and its variegated nature (*citratva*) is the predicate, there would result the consequence of the word expressing the fruit becoming meaningless; or, if both were determined [as predicates], there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Moreover, the expectancy for a fruit regarding the sacrifice under discussion (*prakṛta-yāga*) would remain unfulfilled.

If one were to assume a fruit by means of the *Viśvajit* principle, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), as well as the contingency of a syntactical split due to subverting the established unity of this injunctive sentence with the sentence "curd and honey" (*dadhi-madhu*), which contains no mention of such a fruit.

However, if the word *citrā* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because it merely establishes the connection with a fruit for the ritual action under discussion which requires a fruit; for the word *citrā* is applicable there, since the sacrifice under discussion consists of multiple substances. Thus it is established that, for fear of a syntactical split, the word *citrā* is the name of a ritual action. In the case of "He performs the *agnihotra* oblation" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), the word *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual action on account of a scriptural passage describing its origin (*tatprakhyāśāstra*).
Since there exists a scripture that proclaims and brings about that quality, the term *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual action; so it must be understood.

For indeed, according to the principle that "scripture is purposeful only regarding what is not already established by other means," only that which has not been obtained through another way can be the object of an injunction.

Furthermore, if the word *agnihotra* were an injunction of a subsidiary quality (*guṇavidhi*), that quality which is to be enjoined would already have been established by another scriptural authority.
If one asks how this is so, listen:

first, if it were said that fire is to be enjoined as the locus of the oblation (*homa*) by resorting to a locative compound—namely, "that in which the offering (*hotra*) is made to the fire"—then such an injunction would be purposeless, because that very fact has already been established by the text: "He offers in the *bhavantīya* [fire]."

If it is argued that, by relying on a *caturthī-samāsa* (genitive compound) in the sense of "the office of the Hotṛ for Agni in this [act]," Agni in his form as a deity is thereby established, we say no; because it is already established by another scriptural authority (*śāstrāntara*).

If one asks what that other authority is, some here maintain that the injunction of Agni and Prajāpati is made by another scriptural authority—namely, "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati"—by way of restating the oblation (*homa-anuvāda*), and thus the term *agnihotra* does not itself establish the deity.
Nor is there a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) in the injunction of both [deities].

For if they were enjoined independently of one another, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because the injunctive operation would apply to each separately—as in "He offers to Agni" and "He offers to Prajāpati.
However, since the word *ca* ("and") is not heard, the two words are construed with the verb only as being mutually dependent; thus, there is no syntactical split.

Therefore, by way of restating the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) enjoined in the sentence "He gives a sacrificial fee to the officiating priests," the injunction of cows and so forth—found in the sentence "The cow, the horse, the mule, the donkey, the goat, the sheep, rice, barley, sesame, and beans: his sacrificial fee consists of twelve hundred"—is consistent with the number twelve hundred. This is because there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) since the cows and other items are enjoined as being mutually dependent.
Otherwise, if one were to enjoin several items such as cows and so forth while merely restating the sacrificial fee, it would not be consistent at all.

And although Agni and Prajāpati exist as two deities, there is a conjunction [of them], but not the status of being a deity for the two conjoined together; for this is because a separate case-ending is heard, since the meaning of the particle *ca* (and) is construed with the meaning of the case-ending, and that [case-ending] is primary.
Therefore, Agni and Prajāpati do not have the status of being a deity in the manner of Agni-Soma and the like.
However, other teachers say:

The sentence "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati" does not serve as the means for obtaining Agni [as a deity], because Prajāpati is enjoined by way of restating the oblation (*homānuvāda*).
Nor should it be argued that both are enjoined due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*);
for an injunction enjoins only that which has not been obtained through any other means.

In this regard, just as the evening time is not enjoined by that sentence—because it is already established by another statement, "He offers in the evening"—likewise, Agni is also not enjoined, because he is established by the very wording of the mantra: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Indeed, the wording of a mantra certainly possesses the capacity to present a deity; for this very reason, it is stated that in the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice, Viṣṇu and the others have their status as deities based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*).

But in that case, would there not be a sublation of Agni by Prajāpati as the deity? For it is through the dative case that Prajāpati’s status as the deity is understood, whereas for Agni, it is derived from the wording of the mantra.

In this regard, although there is no specific grammatical rule (smaraṇa) for the dative case in the sense of "deity"—just as there is a rule for the secondary suffix (taddhita) in the sense of "deity" [in the word *śeṣa*]—since the rule "the dative is used for the recipient" (*saṃpradāne caturthī*) prescribes it for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), nevertheless, deityhood (*devatātva*) is simply the state of being intended by the one who offers the sacrifice and so forth. And that state is included within the very nature of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), because the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) consists in being the one who receives while being intended by the one who relinquishes the offering.
Therefore, from the dative case, there is indeed the cognition of deityhood as a constituent part of the recipient.
However, divinity is not understood from the words of the mantra; rather, it is merely the locus [of the deity].
And for this reason, the wording of the mantra is weaker than the dative case-ending.
As they say:

"Whether by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the dative case, or the wording of a mantra, there is an injunction regarding the deity; however, among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding.
Therefore, if it is argued that Agni, who is indicated by a weaker means of knowledge, must be set aside by Prajāpati, who is indicated by a stronger means of knowledge—
True.

There would indeed be sublation if there were a mere injunction of Prajāpati, as in "He offers to Prajāpati. However, Prajāpati, who is being enjoined, is enjoined with reference to the oblation by way of restating Agni, who is not obtained through the wording of the mantra, and with whom he is to be combined. This is because it is simpler to enjoin only Prajāpati combined with him—restating Agni who is obtained from another source—than to enjoin both of them together.
And for this reason, there is no sublation [of one by the other], because there is no injunction that establishes [the two] independently.

Just as in your own view, since Agni and Prajāpati are enjoined with reference to a single oblation, they have an identical purpose; thus, when an option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise result, Prajāpati does not sublate Agni even partially, because their conjunction (*samuccaya*) is enjoined. Similarly, even when Prajāpati is enjoined in conjunction with Agni—who is merely referred to (*anūdya*) because he is not established by the wording of the mantra—there is no sublation; the principle is the same.

As for the objection that, if Agni were established by the wording of the mantra, the evening oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*) would result in having two deities due to the force of the mixed indicative marks in the mantra "Agni is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā," that is not so. For, just as there is an injunction of Prajāpati conjoined with Agni, there is no injunction of Sūrya conjoined [with Agni]; thus, Sūrya—though suggested by the wording of the mantra—is set aside by Prajāpati, who is known through a more powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for the objection that, since Agni’s status as a deity is established by the wording of the mantra itself, the injunction regarding Prajāpati would be accomplished by a single sentence alone—namely, "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati," and "That which one offers in the morning to Sūrya and to Prajāpati"—and thus the division into two sentences would be redundant; that is not so. It would be redundant if the intention were merely to enjoin Prajāpati alone. [In fact,] in the evening oblation, there is an injunction of Prajāpati conjoined with Agni.

In the morning oblation (*prātarhoma*), both the injunction for Prajāpati as gathered together with Sūrya—obtained from the wording of the mantra, "Sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā"—and [the injunction for Prajāpati alone] are intended to be expressed.
This cannot be accomplished by a single sentence;
therefore, the two sentences are meaningful.

As for the claim that if Agni were established by the wording of the mantra—since the mantra-wording "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā" is employed in the evening oblation by the injunction "one offers in the evening"—then Agni, as revealed by that mantra, must also be understood as the deity in that very rite when combined with Prajāpati, and thus the word "evening" (*sāyam*) in the sentence "to Agni and... would be redundant;
and likewise, that the word "morning" (*prātaḥ*) in the sentence "to Sūrya and... would be redundant.
Furthermore, since the wording of the mantra reveals Agni as qualified by the attribute of luminosity (jyotiṣṭva), it is understood that the deity itself is indeed so qualified.

That too is not correct. Even if two deities were enjoined by restating the *homa*, their acquisition would be possible through the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the two mantra-texts themselves, rendering such an injunction purposeless. Furthermore, even if the injunction were intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for those two [deities] excluded by the injunction of the mantra with mixed indicative power, the words "evening" (*sāyam*) and "morning" (*prātar*) occurring within that injunction would be meaningless; for since the two mantras being enjoined are already acquired through a fixed distribution (*vyavasthā*), the deities they manifest are likewise fixed. As for the claim that these are merely restatements (*anuvāda*), that applies equally in both cases.

Even though Agni is known from the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), he alone—not as qualified by an attribute—is the deity. This is because in the sentence "to Agni" (*yad agnaye ca*) and in the passage "the first oblation belongs to Agni," only Agni alone is mentioned, and thus he is understood to be the deity in his unqualified form.

Just as, for instance, in the *upāṃśuyāja*, although Viṣṇu and others are known from the wording of the mantra, they do not become deities as qualified by attributes, because in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently"—only the unqualified one is mentioned; so it is here.

Therefore, since there is no defect in [the mantra] being based on the wording of the mantra, and because enjoining two deities would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*), Prajāpati alone—conjoined with Agni—is enjoined here by referring back to Agni as already established elsewhere.
Furthermore, it cannot be argued that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and that the word *ca* (and) is not redundant;
for the meaning of *ca* is indeed conjunction (*samuccaya*).

If the particle *ca* were to express that conjunction as the primary meaning, then—since a primary element can incorporate multiple qualifiers—there would be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the injunction of the conjunction of two factors, just as there is none in the injunction of a purchase qualified by redness and other attributes.

However, the particle *ca* does not express conjunction as the primary meaning, because it denotes it only as subordinate to another term. For this very reason, in the tenth book [of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra], the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrated the distinction between the particle *ca* and the word "conjunction" (*samuccaya*).

For the word *samuccaya* (conjunction) expresses that [conjunction] primarily, whereas the particle *ca* does not. If it were to express it primarily, then the two factors of action would be connected with the qualities of the action, as in the expressions "the conjunction is beautiful" or "the conjunction is to be seen. Consequently, the usage would have to be "and the *ca* is beautiful" or "and the *ca* is to be seen," just as one says "the conjunction is beautiful" or "the conjunction is to be seen. Furthermore, if the particle *ca* expressed conjunction primarily, just like the word *samuccaya*, then there would also be such usages as "the conjunction of the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," just as one says "the conjunction of the *dhava* and *khadira* trees. However, such usages do not occur. Therefore, the particle *ca* does not denote conjunction primarily. Thus, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It is not the case that the particle *ca* denotes conjunction primarily. This is because the primary denotation of a word is determined by its capacity (*śakti*), and the capacity of the particle *ca* is not observed to reside in the sense of conjunction. For it is observed that the capacity of the word *samuccaya* resides in the sense of conjunction, while the capacity of the particle *ca* resides in the sense of inclusion (*anvācaya*) and so forth. Since the capacity of the particle *ca* is not observed in the sense of conjunction, it cannot be said that the particle *ca* denotes conjunction primarily. Therefore, the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of inclusion and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he eats rice and drinks water," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of inclusion. Moreover, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats barley," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of option (*vikalpa*). And in the expression "he eats rice and he eats ghee," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of sequence (*paurvāparya*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he is a Brahmin and he is not a Kṣatriya," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of exclusion. Moreover, in the expression "he is a Brahmin and he is not a Vaiśya," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). And in the expression "he is a Brahmin and he is not a Śūdra," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of simultaneity (*yugapad*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he eats rice and drinks water at the same time," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of simultaneity. Moreover, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats barley simultaneously," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of coexistence (*sahabhāva*). And in the expression "he eats rice and he eats ghee together," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of aggregation (*samudāya*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats vegetables," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of aggregation. Moreover, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats fruit," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of collection (*saṃgraha*). And in the expression "he eats rice and he eats milk," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of combination (*miśraṇa*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he is a Brahmin and indeed a learned man," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis. Moreover, in the expression "he is a Brahmin and only a Brahmin," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of limitation (*niyama*). And in the expression "he is a Brahmin and certainly a virtuous man," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of certainty (*niścaya*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of distribution (*pratyeka*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats each [type of] vegetable," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of distribution. Moreover, in the expression "he eats rice and he eats each [type of] fruit," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of repetition (*āvṛtti*). And in the expression "he eats rice and he eats each [type of] milk," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of succession (*krama*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of negation (*pratiṣedha*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he is not a Brahmin and he is not a Kṣatriya," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of negation. Moreover, in the expression "he is not a Brahmin and he is not a Vaiśya," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*). And in the expression "he is not a Brahmin and he is not a Śūdra," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "is this a post or a person? the particle *ca* is used in the sense of doubt. Moreover, in the expression "is this silver or mother-of-pearl? the particle *ca* is used in the sense of uncertainty (*anadhyavasāya*). And in the expression "is this a dream or a delusion? the particle *ca* is used in the sense of error (*bhrānti*). Therefore, since the particle *ca* is observed to be used in these various senses, it is not a term for conjunction primarily. Consequently, it is established that the particle *ca* is a term for conjunction only by way of secondary implication. This is the conclusion. Furthermore, the particle *ca* is not a term for conjunction primarily, because it is observed to be used in the sense of purpose (*prayojana*) and so forth. For instance, in the expression "he goes to the village and [for the purpose of] fetching water," the particle *ca* is used in the sense of purpose. Moreover, in the expression
Therefore, the particle *ca* does not express a conjunction as the primary meaning, by which—through the prescription of a single principal element—there would be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Rather, it expresses that [conjunction] precisely as a subordinate element of two factors.

For if there were a prescription of two principal elements, such as "Agni and Prajāpati" joined together, there would necessarily be a syntactical split, just as in the case of the prescription of two Sāmans by Carhaudakeśa.

Even though the particle *ca* primarily expresses conjunction (*samuccaya*), its primary status with respect to two grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is nonetheless untenable. This is because the two factors expressed by case-endings (*vibhakti*) are subordinate to the action (*kriyā*), and thus cannot be subordinate to the conjunction. Indeed, a factor presented by words such as those ending in *kṛt*-suffixes may be connected with something other than the action—for instance, as in the expressions "conjunction of factors" (*kāraka-samuccaya*) or "conjunction of instruments" (*karaṇa-samuccaya*). However, a factor expressed by a case-ending is connected only with the action, since factors are invariably construed with that very action.
Therefore, that which is not expressed by the word *ataḥ* is expressed as subordinate to the *kāraka*;
and two *kārakas* are [here] primary.
Furthermore, when two primary elements are prescribed with reference to a single [word], there is indeed a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
As they have said:
"Even if a single *kāraka* is connected with multiple words, it is nevertheless not expressed by non-repeated suffixes."

As for the claim that there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) when multiple items such as cows and so forth are enjoined by way of restating the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), just as there is none when two factors of action (*kāraka*) are enjoined—that is not correct.

For in the sentence "A cow and a horse," cows and the others are not enjoined by way of restating the sacrificial fee; for, according to the reasoning already stated, this would result in a syntactical split.

Even if the difficulty were somehow avoided by means of the particle *ca* ("and"), there would still be a syntactical split in enjoining both the multiple items such as cows and the number one hundred and twelve.

In the *Ādhvaryava* recension, regarding the passage beginning with "And a cow," it is stated in the tenth [book] that this forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the [passage] "One hundred and twelve for the year" by way of its being a thousandfold.
