Therefore, by this sentence, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) itself is enjoined as qualified by both [attributes]. And because it is an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

For this very reason, Pārthasārathi Miśra stated in various places in the tenth book [of the *Tantravārttika*]: "In that case, it is the [cow] qualified by freedom from fear (*abhaya*) that is enjoined," and "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of many cows and so forth, is enjoined. Nor does this render the injunction "He gives the sacrificial fee to the priests" (*ṛtvigbhyo dakṣiṇāṃ dadāti*) redundant; for that [injunction] is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) or is intended to establish the connection with the priests. Indeed, through the recollection of the word "sacrificial fee," the connection of that [fee] would apply both to the priests (*ṛtvij*) and to the cup-attendants (*camasādhvaryu*).

And this [fault of] sentence-splitting does not occur here, because it was stated in the third [book] that the word *ṛtvij* (priest) applies to the *camasādhvaryus* only insofar as they share the same origin (*tulyajananimittatva*) with the *brahmā* and other priests, and thus they lack the status of being *ṛtvij*s.
Consequently, in the sentence "the cow and the horse," there is no sentence-splitting because it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).

However, in the case of "what one offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati," it is not a qualified injunction, because the oblation (*homa*) is already established by the rule "one performs the *agnihotra*."

Therefore, since prescribing both [deities] as combined by way of restating the *homa* would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and entail excessive complexity (*gaurava*), this sentence does not prescribe two deities. Rather, having referred to Agni as already established by the mantra, Prajāpati is prescribed as combined with him for the purpose of the *homa*. Consequently, this [sentence] is not the source for the attainment of Agni; rather, it is the wording of the mantra itself that establishes him. And since Agni is thus attained through that [mantra], the term *agnihotra* does not serve to provide the deity; what then? It is simply the name [of the sacrifice].
Thus, it is established that the word *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual (*karmanāmadheya*) because of a scripture that declares its identity with that [already known] act.

Likewise, since the deities such as *samit* in the *prayāja* offerings are already established by the wording of mantras—such as "May the *samits*, O Agni, enjoy the clarified butter" (*samidhaḥ samidho agna ājyasya vyantu*)—the words *samit* and so forth in passages like "He sacrifices with the *samits*" (*samidho yajati*) are names of rituals due to a scripture that declares their identity with that [already known] act.
As they say:
Since another scripture does not provide the qualities intended to be enjoined here, its attainment [through that other] would be useless; therefore, it is accepted as a name (*nāmadheya*).
This is the general direction.

In the case of "One desiring to perform malevolent magic should sacrifice with the *śyena*," the word *śyena* is a name for the ritual action because of its designation by that [name]. By "designation by that" is meant comparison; that is to say, it is so because otherwise [the designation] would be inexplicable.
For instance, that which is to be enjoined is the object of praise.

If, in this case, the hawk were the thing to be enjoined, then its praise would have to be performed by means of the explanatory passages (arthavādas). However, the hawk cannot be praised by the explanatory passage through such a comparison as: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hating enemy."
Because the praise of another matter is being performed by means of the comparison with a hawk (*śyena*),

and it is not possible to praise that very same thing by means of the comparison with a hawk— since the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) requires distinct referents—

when a sacrifice designated as "hawk" (*śyena*) is enjoined, its praise can then be effected through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) by means of the comparison with a hawk. Thus, because the word *śyena* is used as a designation for it, it is the name of the sacrifice.

Thus it is established that being a name (*nāmadheya*) results from four causes. Some, however, state that the fifth cause for being a name is the "strength of a quality enjoined at the origin" (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇabalīyastva*); for instance, in the case of the injunction *vaiśvadevena yajeta*, the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of a rite because of the strength of a quality enjoined at the origin. This is because the four previously mentioned causes for being a name are not possible here. To explain:

It cannot be argued that it is not appropriate for this to be a name because of the absence of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possessive meaning); for by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix in the word *vaiśvadevena* itself, the sacrifice—which possesses that [deity]—is already expressed.
For the rule for secondary derivatives is traditionally taught in the sense of "this has that as its deity" (*sā 'syā devatā*).

In this regard, although it is understood from the traditional rule (*smṛti*)—"in the case of a *sūkta* or an oblation (*havis*)"—that the word *asya* (contained within a *taddhita* suffix) has primary denotation with respect to either a *sūkta* or an oblation, nevertheless, because all nouns denote that which is present to the mind, and because neither a *sūkta* nor an oblation is present here, the word *asya* denotes the sacrifice (*yajña*) itself, which is present by virtue of the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). Thus, there is no indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) regarding the sacrifice.
Furthermore, because the single deity Viśvedevas is enjoined, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Nor is it a name (*nāmadheya*) on account of a scriptural passage describing that same [deity] (*tatprakhyaśāstra*).

For where a quality (guṇa) enjoined [by one text] is already obtained from another source, there the status of being a name (nāmadheya) arises due to the "text proclaiming that" (tatprakhya-śāstra), as in the case of the word *agnihotra*. Here, the eight sacrifices beginning with the *āgneya* are the subject under discussion. Among them, although the Viśvedevas are already established for the *āmikṣā* sacrifice by the rule "the *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas," nevertheless, since they are not established for the other seven sacrifices, the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" enjoin them there. Since there is no other "text proclaiming that" by which their status as a name would be determined through such an injunction, [the term *vaiśvadeva* is a name].

Nor should it be said that this [name "Vaiśvadeva"] belongs to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone; for that would result in the redundancy of the sentence, "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. If the word "Vaiśvadeva" were the name of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone, then that very sacrifice would be restated by this [sentence].

But there is no purpose in such a restatement; for the eastern-sloping site, which is enjoined by the rule "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east," can be connected to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice even without this sentence, since it is related to the Viśvedevas.
If, however, [the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice] were the name for all the constituent sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, then the sentence "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" would be purposeless;
for in that case, eight sacrifices would be referred to by it.
And because they are mounted upon a single cognition through this reference (anuvāda), the word *vaiśvadeva* is established as the name for all eight sacrifices taken together.

And thus, in the case of the statement "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east," it is established that by means of the word *vaiśvadeva*, the eight sacrifices are referred to (*anūdya*) and the injunction regarding the ground sloping toward the east is applied to them.
If that [original] sentence did not exist, then by this [present] sentence, the connection with the location sloping toward the east would apply to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone.
Therefore, the purpose of this sentence is precisely to establish the connection with the location sloping toward the east for all eight sacrifices.

Thus, the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name for all eight [offerings]. Nor is it possible for a scriptural injunction (*tatprakhyā-śāstra*) to be the basis for that [designation] there, because the Viśvedevas are not established in seven [of the offerings]; therefore, the word *vaiśvadeva* does not function as a name on account of such an injunction.
Nor is it [a name] "on account of its designation" (*tadvyapadeśāt*), because no such designation is observed.

Therefore, since the four aforementioned modes are not the cause for the word *vaiśvadeva* being a name (*nāmadheya*), the only cause is the strength of a quality prescribed at the origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa-baliyastva*). To explain: in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*," it is first of all not possible to enjoin a deity by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to a non-contextual action, because those [actions] are not present here.

Nor is it possible that this constitutes an injunction for a different ritual action characterized by a distinct deity, as that would entail unnecessary complexity (gaurava) and would contradict the indicative mark (liṅga) in the phrase "eight oblations," which otherwise has no other application.
Therefore, it must be stated that by means of this [text], deities are enjoined with reference to the ritual actions under discussion.

In that regard, since the Viśvedevas are already established in the sacrifice involving the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture, it must be stated that the Viśvedevas are enjoined by this sentence in respect to the remaining seven sacrifices.
And that is not possible, because those [sacrifices] are already occupied by the Agni and other deities prescribed at their origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
For a connection occurs through mutual requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*);
since the requirement for a deity in the case of the Āgneya and other sacrifices is satisfied by the very Agni and others prescribed at their origin, it is not logical to enjoin Viśvedevas therein.
Therefore, because of the superior strength of a quality [guṇa] taught at the time of origination (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of the ritual action.
As they say:
"Because it is already occupied by another quality, no other quality can find a place; nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) due to inequality; therefore, it is appropriate that it be a name alone."
Other teachers, however, say:

when a word conveys a connection with a certain quality in a particular ritual action, and if that connection is established by another scriptural authority (*śāstrāntara*), then that word is the name (*nāmadheya*) for that action because of the "scripture proclaiming it" (*tatprakhya-śāstra*). And as for whether that other scripture is an injunction (*vidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there is no concern regarding that distinction here.
In that context, regarding the term *agnihotra*, another scriptural passage that does not convey a connection with fire is itself the injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, the term *vaiśvadeva* conveys a connection with the Viśvedevas in the ritual action;

and this connection with the Viśvedevas is understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which states: "Because the Viśvedevas sacrificed together, that is the *vaiśvadeva*-ness of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice," thus applying to the eight sacrifices.
Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever that only an injunction (*vidhi*)—and not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—can constitute a "text proclaiming that" (*tatprakhya-śāstra*).

For this very reason, in the case of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the word *Jyotiṣṭoma* is established as a name (*nāmadheya*) by virtue of the "text proclaiming that," because it functions for one desiring heaven based on the connection with "lights" (*jyotis*) understood from the explanatory passage: "These indeed are the lights which are its *stomas*.
The same should be understood in the present case as well, since there is no evidence for postulating a fifth category [of names].
For this very reason, in the section concerning the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the author of the Vārttika concluded thus:

"The status of all [these terms] as names is established precisely by the principle of *tatprakhyatā* (being known from that). Furthermore, the statement regarding the superior strength of a quality prescribed in the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) is merely an additional argument to support the impossibility of those terms being injunctive of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
Thus it is established that, by virtue of a scriptural passage descriptive of that [deity], the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

Now, an objection is raised: in the section concerning the animal and Soma sacrifices (*paśusomādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that in such cases as "He takes [the cup] for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*), there is no assumption of a sacrifice (*yajati*), because of the direct hearing of the word "sacrifice" in the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*).

By that same logic, let there be no assumption of a sacrifice here in the case of "The curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*), since the word "sacrifice" is directly heard in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" (*vaiśvadevena yajeta*).
If it is argued: "Let there be, by this very sentence, an injunction for a ritual action qualified by a deity;
and when that [action] requires a substance, let there be an injunction for the substance, namely, 'the *āmikṣā* for the *vaiśvadeva*.

In this way, neither of the two sentences would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), nor would there be a conflict with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the statement 'there are eight oblations' (*aṣṭau havīṃṣi*), which otherwise would have no other recourse."
It is not so. Regarding the statement "the *āmikṣā* [curd-mixture] is for the Viśvedevas," one must explain what is being enjoined by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If the substance were enjoined by way of a restatement of the Viśvedevas, the substance would only be a subordinate element of the deity, and not a subordinate element of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, it has been stated that because the word *vaiśvadevī* is a *taddhita* derivative denoting a deity, it expresses the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) as its very essence.

In that context, the prescription of the substance by means of the word *vaiśvadevī* must be performed precisely through that term, because of the direct hearing of the word (*padaśruti*). Just as in the case of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the presentation of the instrument is performed by the verbal root alone due to the direct hearing of the word, and not by the prefix or secondary member—as was stated in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*—so it is here.
Moreover, in this regard, there is no contradiction with the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā*), as seen in the rule: "The first portion is for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*."
Therefore, even when restating the sacrifice (*yāga*), one must necessarily assume the verb "to sacrifice" (*yajati*) in the passage *vaiśvadevy āmikṣā* for the purpose of enjoining the material.

Consequently, there is a disparity with the logic of the sections concerning the animal (*paśu*) and the Soma. This is because, in the case of *aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*, since it enjoins the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*) qualified by a deity, no sacrifice is assumed; whereas, given that a sacrifice must be assumed here, it is more appropriate to enjoin an action qualified by both material and deity in the very passage *vaiśvadevy āmikṣā*, as no other [material] is heard in connection with it.

In this way, through sentences such as "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" and "the porridge for Soma," the uniformity of the sequence of the Vaiśvadeva section—specifically the sentence regarding the *āmikṣā*—is preserved.

Otherwise, there would result a structural inconsistency: in all those [preceding] cases, there would be an injunction of a sacrifice established by the connection between a material and a deity, whereas here there would be an injunction of the material alone.

Furthermore, if the word *vaiśvadeva* in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*" were to serve merely to designate a deity, then the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"Because the Viśvedevas sacrificed together, that is the *vaiśvadeva*-ness of the *vaiśvadeva*"—would be entirely without basis.

For it is from this very *arthavāda* that we understand the word *vaiśvadeva* to be applied to the rite by virtue of its having been performed by the Viśvedevas, and not by virtue of designating a deity.

Moreover, if "one should sacrifice with the *vaiśvadeva*" were a mere injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga-vidhi*), then curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) would not possess the status of being taught at the time of the rite's origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭatva*).

And thus, since the whey (*vājina*) cannot be excluded by that [curd-mixture, *āmikṣā*], both the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* would have to be constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice. Consequently, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between them; and such an option is subject to eight logical fallacies (*aṣṭadoṣa*).

Therefore, the injunction of the sacrifice is contained precisely in the passage "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas," while the other [mention of the *vājina*] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
And as for its being a restatement (*anuvāda*), it has already been explained how it is not purposeless; so let that matter rest for now.
Thus, it is established that the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*).

Therefore, by means of this fourfold investigation—beginning with the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—it has been demonstrated that a name possesses purposefulness by way of delimiting the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*).
Prohibitions possess a connection to human goals by virtue of causing a person to desist from actions that lead to what is undesirable.
For instance:

Just as injunctions (*vidhi*), by expressing an impulsion (*pravartana*), imply that the enjoined act—such as a sacrifice—is a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhana*) in order to fulfill their own nature as impellers, and thereby incite a person toward that act; so too do prohibitions (*niṣedha*), such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," by expressing a cessation (*nivartana*), imply that the prohibited act—such as eating *kalañja*—is a cause of misfortune (*anartha-hetutva*) in order to fulfill their own nature as preventers, and thereby restrain a person from that act.
[Objection: But how can prohibitions be understood to convey a cessation?

To the extent that in cases such as "one should not eat" or "one should not kill," when the meaning of the negative particle—namely, non-existence—is construed directly with the meaning of the verbal root, the sentence-meaning understood in every instance is simply the necessity of avoiding the action expressed by the root.

Consequently, just as in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and similar injunctions the sentence-meaning is the necessity of performing the sacrifice, so too in prohibitions the sentence-meaning is the necessity of avoiding the respective action denoted by the root, and not the act of cessation itself.

It is not so; for even in the absence of an intervention, it is impossible for the meaning of the verbal root—which has appeared as subordinate to the meaning of the suffix—to be construed with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Indeed, that which is subordinate to one thing cannot be construed with another; otherwise, in the sentence "Bring the king's man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), the king would also be construed with the act of bringing.

Consequently, even though there is no intervention [between them], the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Just as the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) does not connect with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), so too the objects denoted by words such as *kalañja* do not connect [with the negative]; for these also are presented as subordinate to a case-role (*kāraka*), and thus it is impossible for the meaning of the negative particle, which resides in a separate word, to connect with them. Just as the one-year-old cow connects with the quality of redness, so too, because it cannot connect with anything else, the meaning of the negative particle connects with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). This is because that [suffix-meaning] is predominant, just as the qualities such as redness connect with the efficient force of action (*kriyābhāvanā*).

Even there, [the negative particle] does not connect with the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*), which is denoted by the verbal suffix portion; for that too is presented as subordinate to the instigation (*pravartanā*) denoted by the optative suffix portion (*liṅtva*).
Therefore, the negative particle connects with the optative suffix portion, because that is the most predominant element in relation to everything else.
And it is the very nature of the negative particle to convey the opposite of that which is connected to it.

For in the case of "it is not" (*nāsti*), the negative particle (*nañ*)—when connected with the word "existent" (*asti*) which denotes existence—conveys non-existence, which is the opposite of existence.
Here, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ-artha*) is, first of all, instigation (*pravartanā*).

Therefore, when the negative particle is connected with that, it conveys cessation (*nivartanā*), which is the opposite of instigation. This is because, just as upon hearing a sentence [of injunction] one understands the instigation in the form "this [speaker] is impelling me," so too upon hearing a prohibitive sentence, one understands cessation in the form of an activity conducive to desisting, namely, "this [speaker] is turning me away."
Therefore, in all prohibitions, the meaning of the sentence consists solely in the turning away [from an action].
In this way, it is established that injunctions and prohibitions have distinct meanings.
However, on the view that the meaning of the sentence is the duty to refrain from killing and so forth, since it is the duty itself that is conveyed in both cases, they would have the same meaning.
And that is not tenable,
as they say:
"Whatever difference is seen in the world between the killing of a Brahmin and the horse sacrifice, exactly such a difference exists here between injunctions and prohibitions."
Thus:

"Likewise, there is a distinction between injunctions and prohibitions because they are absolutely distinct in five ways: by way of their fruit, their cognition, their object of knowledge, their qualified practitioners, and their expressive capacity."
Thus,

even in the view where the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) is "being a means to what is desired" (iṣṭasādhanatva), the negative particle (nañ) conjoined with that optative suffix conveys "being a means to what is undesired" (aniṣṭasādhanatva), which is the opposite of being a means to what is desired.
In every case, however, because the negative particle is the primary element, it is construed with the suffix.

But when there is some sublation (bādhaka) regarding its connection with that [the agent], then, having no other recourse, the connection is with the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha). And that sublation is of two kinds:
the introductory statement "This is his vow" (tasya vratam), and the contingency of an alternative (vikalpa).
And by those two types of sublation, there occurs a resort to *paryudāsa* (exclusion) in sentences when [the negation] functions as an object;
in the absence of that, it is simply a *pratiṣedha* (prohibition).

"That is to be known as *paryudāsa* where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the following word," and "that is to be known as *pratiṣedha* where the negative particle is connected with the verb."
And such is the definition of those two.
In that regard, in passages such as "one should not look at the rising or setting sun," recourse is taken to *paryudāsa* (exclusion), because of the introductory statement, "that is his vow.
For it is thus:
By the word *vrata*, that which is to be performed (*kartavya*) is denoted.

Consequently, since the text begins with the statement of the duties (*kartavyārtha*) of a *snātaka*, when the expectation arises as to "what is that which must be performed?", the very thing to be performed must be stated in the subsequent passage beginning with "he shall not look at the rising [sun]," and so forth; for one must express what is required by the context.
If a different matter were stated, the preceding sentence would lack completeness (*sākāṅkṣatva*) and would thus be invalid (*aprāmāṇya*).

For if a matter that ought to be performed is introduced as the subject to be stated at the beginning and is not subsequently expressed, it is impossible for the preceding sentence to be free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).

Nor can that which possesses expectancy possess authority (*prāmāṇya*), because that consequence would then apply even to such statements as "cow, horse, man. Furthermore, if the verb "one should look" were to have its meaning understood through the introductory context, there could be no mention of a different object.
Therefore, in this sentence, some action that must be performed must indeed be stated.

And when such an action is stated, the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the suffix is not possible, because if it were connected to the suffix, the statement of an action to be performed would be untenable. Thus, the negative particle, having been detached from the suffix, is connected with the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with that [the nominal stem], it does not possess the quality of negation; for its status as a negator arises only through connection with a prescriptive element (*vidhāyaka*), since being a negator is the very opposite of being prescriptive.
However, when joined with a noun (*nāman*) or a verbal root (*dhātu*), the negative particle does not function as a negator, because those two are not prescriptive. As they say:

However, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a noun or a verbal root-meaning, it is not at all a negator [in the sense of mere absence]. For instance, *abrāhmaṇa* (non-Brahmin) and *adharma* (non-dharma) denote respectively what is merely different from a Brahmin and what is opposed to dharma. Consequently, in the case of *na īkṣeta* ("one should not look"), because the negative particle is connected with the verbal root, a certain meaning that is opposed to looking is conveyed by both the negative particle and the root *īkṣ*. Now, even though there is a traditional rule stating that "the negative particle [expresses] otherness (*tadanya*), opposition (*tadviruddha*), and absence (*tadbhāva*)," the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the negative particle resides only in the absence (*abhāva*) of that which it is connected with, due to parsimony (*lāghava*). It does not reside in "otherness" or "opposition," because those two involve the concept of absence and are thus more complex (*gaurava*), and because it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings.

If it is argued that, therefore, when the negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with a verbal root, its function is solely to convey the absence of the root's meaning, and not to convey a meaning contrary to it—
this is true;
the primary denotation (*śakti*) of the negative particle is indeed absence alone.
The mention of "recollection" (smaraṇa), however, intends the sense of "depending upon" (pratītya) and not the sense of "capacity" (śakti).
Even the phrase "connected with the meaning of the verbal root and the name" intends the sense of "depending upon.
Nevertheless, in the case of "one does not look" (ne 'kṣeta), because the suffix is not connected with the negative particle (nañ), some meaning must be enjoined by it.
In that case, first of all, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) cannot be enjoined, because its absence is understood through the negative particle (*nañ*).
Nor can its absence be enjoined, because an absence is not something fit to be enjoined.

Therefore, by means of the negative particle and the verb *īkṣati*, some meaning other than the act of seeing—which is incompatible with it—is conveyed through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as that which is fit to be enjoined.

If an object perceived as being incompatible with sight is not seen, that is the "volition of non-seeing" (*anīkṣaṇa-saṃkalpa*). This is because of its incompatibility with sight; for even though other objects may also be incompatible with sight, the volition itself is defined by the destruction of all [other] activities.
That very volition is enjoined here as something to be performed in the phrase "he does not look," meaning: "One should bring about [the state] through the volition of non-seeing.
And when there is a requirement for a result (*bhāvya*), the destruction of sin—known from the supplementary passage, "By this much he becomes separated from evil"—is connected as that result.

And thus, because the resolution for the purpose of destroying evil is enjoined here as something to be performed, its syntactic unity with the phrase "that is his vow" (*tasya vratam*) is established.
Therefore, it is proven that in the case of the injunction "he does not look [at the sun]," one must resort to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), since the section begins with "that is his vow.
In the case of "he does not perform the *yeyajāmaha* at the *anuyāja* offerings," however, one resorts to that [exclusion] because an option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise result.

For instance: if, due to the desire for connection with the principal element (*pradhāna*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is accepted as being connected to the suffix (*pratyaya*), then it must be stated that by this sentence the *yeyajāmahe* formula is prohibited in the *anuyāja* offerings; that is, "one should not perform the *yeyajāmahe* in the *anuyājas*. However, a prohibition of that [formula] therein is not possible without its prior application (*prāpti*), because a prohibition is dependent upon such application. For this very reason, the statement "not in the intermediate space, not in the sky" does not function as a prohibition, because the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) is not applicable in the intermediate space or in the sky.
For this very reason, it is logically consistent that the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" functions as a restriction (*niyamavidhi*) for the purpose of turning one away from killing.
For every person sometimes engages in killing and the like, and at other times, due to the absence of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, does not engage in them.

In that context, if the prohibition did not depend upon such engagement (*prāptisāpekṣatva*), then since the authority of the scripture would be established only with respect to a person who has refrained from killing by suppressing passion and the like, a man who has engaged in killing through passion and the like would have no reason to desist from it.

However, if prohibitory injunctions depend upon the attainment [of an occasion], they do not apply to one who has not spontaneously engaged in an action, because there is no possibility of such engagement; rather, they apply only to one who has already engaged through passion and the like. In that case, the prohibitory injunction functions by subduing the passion caused by delusion, and thus the cessation from that activity is logical.

Consequently, the prohibition "A Brahmin must not be killed" conveys a restrictive rule regarding desisting from action (*nivṛttiniyama*), just as the injunction "One should thresh the rice" conveys a restrictive rule regarding threshing (*avaghātaniyama*).

Just as the scriptural injunction "one should thresh the rice" does not apply to a person who has already begun threshing for the purpose of removing the husk—because it would be redundant—but rather applies to one who might instead proceed to splitting the grain or similar acts; so too, the scriptural injunction "one should not kill" does not apply to a person who has spontaneously desisted from killing—because it would be redundant—but rather applies to a person who is engaged in killing, because it prohibits that which was about to be performed, meaning: "that which was to be done, do not do."
And therefore, since prohibitions depend upon prior application, when there is a prohibition of the *yeyajāmaha* in the *anuyāja* offerings, its application to those offerings must be stated.
Furthermore, that application cannot possibly arise from passion (*rāga*)—as it does, for example, in the case of gambling and the like;
rather, it must be stated as arising from the scriptural injunction: "One performs the *yeyajāmaha* in sacrifices."

Furthermore, if there were a prohibition of that which has been established by a scriptural rule, there would be an option (vikalpa), because it is impossible for one scriptural rule to absolutely sublate another scriptural rule in the same way that a scriptural rule [prohibiting] passion sublates the passion caused by delusion. Nor should it be argued that the general rule—"In sacrifices, he performs the *yeyajāmahe* [formula]"—is sublated by the specific rule—"Not in the *anuyāja* offerings"—just as the rule concerning the *āhavanīya* fire is sublated by the rule concerning the word "pada.

For the relationship of the sublated and the sublater between two scriptural rules exists only where they are mutually independent; indeed, the rule concerning the word "pada" has no need to depend on the rule concerning the *āhavanīya* fire for the sake of enjoining its own meaning.

However, the prohibitory scripture has a requirement for the injunction, "In sacrifices, one performs the *yeyajāmahe*," for the sake of its incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Thus, just as the prohibitory scripture possesses strength due to its specific scope, the injunctive scripture likewise possesses strength by virtue of being that upon which the former depends; therefore, it is not proper for the injunction to be completely sublated by the prohibition. Consequently, because it is both enjoined and prohibited, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), and that too is not tenable.
For if there were an option between alternatives, the authority of the scripture would be undermined.

Indeed, the authority of the injunction "one should not perform the *yeyajāmaha* at the *anuyāja*s" could not be maintained if one were to perform the *yeyajāmaha* at the *anuyāja*s—just as the authority of the rule regarding *yava* grain cannot be maintained at the time of performing the rite with *vrīhi* grain. Furthermore, there would be the postulation of two unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*).
For it is understood from the injunction that some benefit (*upakāra*) arises from the performance of the *yeyajāmaha* formula in the *anuyāja* offerings;

and it is understood from the prohibition that [this benefit] arises from its non-performance, just as [the benefit of avoiding the sin of falsehood arises] in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices from the non-utterance of untruth. And since that benefit would be of an invisible nature (*adṛṣṭarūpa*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of postulating two distinct types of invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, a conceptual construction (vikalpa) is not tenable; nor is it appropriate to rely on a simple negation (pratiṣedha), because that would lead to the same undesirable consequence. Rather, relying on the connection of the negative particle (nañ) with the word *anuyāja*, a preclusion (paryudāsa) is adopted, since the two terms—the negative particle and the word *anuyāja*—indicate by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) that which is distinct from the *anuyājas*.
"He performs the *yeyajāmaha* except in the *anuyāja*s.

In this sentence, the *yeyajāmaha* is not enjoined as something to be performed, because it has already been enjoined by the rule: "He performs the *yeyajāmaha* in the *yajati*s. Rather, by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *yeyajāmaha* enjoined by the general rule, its scope is restricted to instances other than the *anuyāja*s.
"In whatever sacrifices one performs the *yeyajāmahe* [utterance], that is [to be done] except in the *anuyāja*s.

Thus, since the general rule—which requires a specific qualification—is provided with its scope as "except in the *anuyāja*s" by this [prohibition], the performance of the *yeyajāmahe* is established as being required in sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s.
However, in the case of the *anuyāja*s, it is neither established as something to be performed nor is it prohibited; therefore, there is no option (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, because the term [‘non-anuyājas’] is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to objects other than the *anuyājas*, the sentence “not in the *anuyājas*” does not lack authority. Therefore, there is no obstacle to adopting an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Thus it is established that in the sentence “not in the *anuyājas*,” one must resort to exclusion because there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*). Now, an objection: if an exclusion is adopted, since the rule “he performs the *yeyajāmaha* in sacrifices” establishes the *yeyajāmaha* for sacrifices in general, and the phrase “not in the *anuyājas*” restricts it to those other than the *anuyājas*, would there not be no difference between exclusion and limitation (*upasaṃhāra*)? For both would result in the same narrowing of scope.

For restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) occurs when that which has been obtained in a general sense is limited to a particular instance. If it is argued that—just as the rule "one divides the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into four parts" applies generally to all *puroḍāśas*, but is restricted to the *āgneya* cake by the rule "one divides the *āgneya* into four parts"—[restriction does not apply here], we say no; for restriction has the purpose of limiting [the application] to that alone. Some maintain that exclusion (*paryudāsa*) has the purpose of limiting [the application] to everything other than that.
Others, however, hold that what is called restriction is a specific function of an injunction consisting in the limitation of what is obtained in a general sense to a particular instance.

As for exclusion (*paryudāsa*): "Exclusion is to be understood as that case where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the subsequent member"—according to this statement by the learned, there is a connection of the *nañ* with either a verbal root or a nominal stem distinct from the suffix.
Consequently, the difference between these two [negations] is indeed clear from their very nature.
Even so, a lack of distinction might be suspected if, wherever there is exclusion, there were necessarily a restatement (*upasaṃhāra*).
And this is not the case; for in such instances as "one should not look at the rising [sun]," even though that [general rule] exists, there is no restriction (upasaṃhāra).

Indeed, in those cases, unlike the fourfold division of the *āgneya* cake, nothing established in a general sense is restricted to a particular instance, because what is enjoined is merely the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) not to look, with the destruction of sin as its purpose.

In the present example, however, since the *ye-yajāmahe* formula—established for the sacrifice in general—is restricted to those other than the *anuyāja* offerings, the injunction can indeed function as a restrictive injunction (*upasaṃhāra-vidhi*). There is nothing contradictory in this much.
For if there were no injunction, how could the function of an injunction—namely, restriction (upasaṃhāra)—be performed by means of exclusion (paryudāsa)? Thus, there would be a contradiction.
Yet, there is no lack of an injunction here; for since the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the word *anuyāja*, the injunctive power of the injunction remains unimpaired.
For in this case, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) serves to provide a scope distinct from the *anuyājas*, just like the word *āgneya*; however, it is the injunction itself that performs the restriction.
Nor should it be argued that there is no "withdrawal" (upasaṃhāra) here because there is an absence of restriction to that alone;
for what is the meaning of "restriction to that alone"?
Does it mean restriction to the Āgneya sacrifice alone, or does it mean the restriction of what is generally obtained to a particular instance alone?

In the first case, there would be no restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *saptadaśya* (the rule of seventeen) taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhita*) by the sentence situated within the context of the Mitravindā sacrifice and others, because there is no limitation upon it regarding the Āgneya [offering].

In the second case, however, just as the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*)—which applies to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in general—is restricted to the Āgneya, so too would there be a restriction to non-anuyāja offerings of that which applies commonly to both anuyājas and non-anuyājas; this is indeed the case.
The distinction, however, is as follows:
In sentences such as "the Āgneya [offering]," the specific elements like the Āgneya are presented by their own words;
however, in the present case, its presentation occurs through exclusion (paryudāsa).
The principle of restatement (upasaṃhāra), however, remains exactly the same.

As for the claim that "because exclusion (*paryudāsa*) has the purpose of restricting [the application] to something other than that," that is not correct; for even though there is an exclusion in the case of "one should not look" (*nekṣeta*), there is no restriction.

Indeed, what was applicable to the general case here is not restricted to something other than that, because it has been stated that this is a prescription of mere intention (*saṃkalpa*). Let this matter rest for now.

Thus it is established that in the case of the rule "not in the *anuyāja*s," one resorts to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) because of the resulting possibility of an option (*vikalpa*). However, where that [exclusion] cannot be resorted to, there one resorts to a prohibition (*niṣedha*) even when that [option] results;
as in the case of "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*."

For here, in the case of the statement "one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] at the *atirātra*," the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin*, which is established by scripture, is prohibited. Although an option (*vikalpa*) would result because it is both enjoined and prohibited, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is not resorted to because it is impossible.

If the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word *ṣoḍaśin* were accepted here, then the meaning of the sentence would be "one takes [something] other than the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra*.
In that case, there would be a contradiction with the direct injunction: "one takes the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra*."
For this very reason, the negative particle (*nañ*) cannot be connected with the word *atirātra*, because that would contradict the direct injunction: "At the *atirātra*, one takes the *ṣoḍaśin*.

Consequently, since an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is untenable here, a simple prohibition (*niṣedha*) alone is accepted; furthermore, an option (*vikalpa*) is admitted, as in the case of the *anuyāja* offerings. And thus, this [point] is established.

A prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) occurs where there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) arising from the initial statement, such as "his vow," and so forth—for example, "One should not eat *kalañja*. Alternatively, a prohibition occurs where, even though an option might arise, it is impossible to resort to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), as in "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice.
However, this much is the distinction [between these two types of prohibition].

Where there is a prohibition that allows for an option (*vikalpa*), the prohibited act does not have the nature of being a cause of misfortune (*anartha-hetutva*), because both the injunction and the prohibition serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*).

However, where no option arises, and the attainment [of the act] occurs through passion while the prohibition serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), there the prohibited act has the nature of being a cause of misfortune; as, for example, in the case of eating *kalañja* (a type of forbidden food).

In cases such as "The initiated one does not give, he does not offer oblations," although acts like giving and offering oblations are established by scripture, they are already established as serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Since they are prohibited here as serving the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), there is no possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) because their purposes are not identical. Nevertheless, these acts do not become causes of misfortune (*anartha*), because there is no establishment [of them] through passion (*rāga*). Even when something established through passion is prohibited for the sake of the sacrifice, the performance of it results in a deficiency of the sacrifice (*kratuvaiguṇya*), but not in the production of misfortune—as is the case with prohibitions such as approaching one's own wife.

The general direction is this: when that which has been obtained through passion is prohibited because it is not a human goal (puruṣārtha), the very thing being prohibited becomes a cause of misfortune (anartha).
Thus, it is established that prohibitions are connected to the human goal.
In this way, the entire Veda is likewise connected to the human goal.
Let us return to the subject at hand.

Thus, just as injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, which are included within the injunction to study, are not purposeless, so too it is untenable that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are purposeless simply because they are included therein. Furthermore, since there is no purpose in their merely conveying their own literal meaning, it must be stated that they culminate in a purposeful meaning through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And these explanatory passages are of two kinds: those supplementary to injunctions and those supplementary to prohibitions.

In that regard, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," which are supplementary to injunctions like "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," possess purposefulness by way of praising the matter to be enjoined. However, explanatory passages such as "He wept," which are supplementary to prohibitions like "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*"), possess purposefulness by way of censuring the thing prohibited.
Consequently, excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood through explanatory passages by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And that knowledge of commendability is connected as the *itikartavyatā* (procedure) within the verbal *bhāvanā*.
This is the main subject at hand.

Thus it is established that the verbal *bhāvanā*—which has the *bhāvanā* of the meaning to be expressed as its objective (*bhāvya*), the cognition of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) etc. as its instrument (*karaṇa*), and the knowledge of commendability as its procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—is denoted by the factor of "optativity" (*liṅtva*).
Now, what is this verbal productive energy (śābdī bhāvanā)?
It is said:
it is a specific operation conducive to the activity of a person.
That alone is the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*),
because there is an invariable cognition that "this [optative suffix] and so forth impels me.
As for the claim that being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is the meaning of the injunction, that is not correct.
If that were the case, the word "iṣṭasādhana" (means of accomplishing the desired) would be a synonym for the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*).

Yet synonymy is not tenable, because they are used together—as in "The twilight worship is a means of accomplishing the desired; therefore, perform it"—and synonyms are never employed simultaneously. Therefore, the meaning of an injunction is specifically a particular kind of activity (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*).
And that [efficient force] in the world is a particularity residing in a person, consisting of a mental disposition (*bhāvanā*).
But in the Veda, since there is no person, it has been stated that it resides solely in the word itself, being synonymous with "impulsion" (*preraṇā*).

If it is objected: "But how can that [force], which is synonymous with impulsion and resides in the word in the world, be understood from a prescriptive word (*vidhiśabda*), given that there is no usage of the word [in such a way] and thus no means of grasping its expressive power (*śakti*)?"—this is true.

Nevertheless, the child first ascertains that the mother’s activity in providing breast milk and so forth is produced by a knowledge of an instigation (*pravartanā*) in the form of his own intention, based on her responding to his own crying and other such acts. Then, observing the activity of the elder who is being prompted occurring immediately after hearing the prompter’s sentence accompanied by a command, he infers that the cause of that activity is the prompter’s knowledge of an instigation.

Although it is reasonable to conclude that even the activity of the prompted elder is preceded by a cognition of the means to a desired end—since one's own activity toward eating and so forth is observed to be preceded by such a cognition—nevertheless, because the activity of the prompted elder is an activity induced by another (just as the mother’s activity was seen to be produced by a cognition of an instigation), it is determined that the cause of that activity is specifically the cognition of an instigation (*pravartanājñāna*).
And he determines that this knowledge of instigation (*pravartanājñāna*) is produced by the injunctive sentence through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvayavyatireka*).
Furthermore, by means of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), he establishes the capacity for injunction (*vidhiśakti*) within that instigation.
Instigation is an operation conducive to activity (*pravṛtti*).

Since that activity—consisting of various forms such as commands (*praiṣa*) and the like—is diverse, it is impossible for each specific form to be denotable by the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) due to their mutual exclusivity. Therefore, one concludes that only the universal property of instigation (*pravartanā-sāmānya*) is what is denoted by the word "injunction.

Consequently, upon hearing an injunction, the intention of the speaker in the form of a command and so forth is understood only in its capacity as instigation, not in its specific form; this is because the apprehension of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*) occurs precisely in that way.
As for the understanding of it in its specific form, that occurs only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And thus, even upon hearing the *liṅ* suffix and other such [verbal endings] in the Veda, only a general "impelling" (*pravartanā*) is perceived.

When the question arises as to what that specific operation (*vyāpāra*) is, since a speaker’s intention—consisting of a command (*praiṣa*) and so forth—is impossible in the impersonal Veda, it is postulated that there is some operation residing in the word itself, which is synonymous with "impulsion" (*preraṇā*). Therefore, the operation residing in the word itself, synonymous with impulsion, is the verbal productive energy (*śābdī bhāvanā*).
And this very thing, as the nature of instigation (*pravartanātva*), is the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*).
This is precisely the meaning of the *Vārttika* passage: "The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express a distinct *bhāvanā*, namely the *abhidhā-bhāvanā*."
Based on the etymological derivation "that by which something is denoted" (*abhidhīyate 'nena*), the word *abhidhā* refers to the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*).
From this [etymology], the teachers say that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), whose essence is the operation of that [injunctive word], is what is expressed by the verbal root and so forth.
Others, however, say:

The meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is instigation (*pravartanā*), which is common to all [forms of prompting] because its capacity is apprehended in that very way. Instigation is an activity conducive to action.

And since in the Veda—which is not of human origin—such things as commands (*praiṣa*) are impossible, some specific kind of activity conducive to human action must be postulated; for the general property of instigation denoted by the word "injunction" cannot reach completion without a particular instance.

In this regard, when the question arises as to what that specific operation (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*) is, it is postulated to be precisely the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), because even that is conducive to activity (*pravṛtti*). For everyone, having understood that something is a means to a desired end, engages in action;
even one prompted by another does not act at all if they do not know that it is a means to a desired end.

Even in the theory that the instigation is independent (*svatantra-preraṇāvāda*), the ignorance of the means being conducive to the desired end (*saṃhitasādhanatvajñāna*) as implied by that [instigation] is indeed admitted; otherwise, the capacity of the injunction to impel action (*pravartakatva*) would be untenable.
Therefore, because it is necessary, the state of being a means conducive to the desired end alone, in its form as "instigation" (*pravartanātva*), is the meaning of the injunction.
And thus, it is established that the word expressing an injunction is well-known in common usage as denoting an operation residing in something else.
Furthermore, one must postulate a single operation called "sound" that is distinct from vibration and the like.

Furthermore, rather than postulating—on the grounds that it is simpler and more parsimonious—that (1) that which is established as the cause for one's own activity or for activity dependent on another is known in the form of "instigation" (*pravartanā*) and possesses a conduciveness to activity; (2) that which is established as making known the operation residing in another is the indicator of its own operation, as in the case of a command (*śakta*); and (3) that the meaning of the verbal root possesses a "conjoined means" (*saṃhitasādhana*) in order to effect the instigating power of the injunction—it is better to postulate that the very thing already necessary, namely the "conjoined means," which is established as the cause of one's own activity, is the meaning of the injunction in the form of "instigation. This is because [the alternative] would involve dependence on something else.

Nor should it be argued that, in order to maintain the instigative character (*pravartakatva*) of the injunction (*vidhi*), one must assume that the means are conducive to a desired end (*saṃhitasādhanatva*); for if instigation were not denoted, the injunction would lack its instigative character, and there would be no basis at all for assuming that the meaning of the verbal root is conducive to a desired end. This is because, even in that [opponent’s] view, the injunction possesses its instigative character precisely through the denotation of instigation (*pravartanā*), and since the general category of instigation denoted by the injunction cannot be fully realized without a specific instance, it necessarily implies that the means are conducive to a desired end.

It should not be argued that if the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), then the simultaneous usage of the forms "the twilight worship is a means to a desired end for you" and "you, perform that" would be untenable. This is because "being a means to a desired end" is not denoted by the injunction in its specific form, but rather in the form of "impelling" (*pravartanātva*).
Furthermore, the co-usage of a general term with a specific term is observed in cases such as "Drupada, the king of the Pañcālas.
Therefore, it is precisely "being a means to a desired end" that constitutes the meaning of the injunction in the form of "impelling."
And that very [activity] is expressed by that form or word; thus it is the verbal *bhāvanā*.
This is precisely the intended meaning of the aforementioned Vārttika as well:

"That which is expressed is the denotation (*abhidhā*), namely the state of having the means [of accomplishment] conjoined [with the end]. That very [denotation], when expressed as an instigation (*pravartanā*), brings about the activity of the person; therefore it is called *bhāvanā*. The roots such as *lī* (to dissolve) express that."
As they say:

"For men, there is no other motivator for actions than the fact that [the action] is a desired means; and they declare that the dharma which is the cause of engagement is the *pravartanā* (incitement).
Therefore, it is established that in the expression 'one should sacrifice' (*yajeta*), the verbal *bhāvanā* is expressed by the element of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)."
The objective productive energy (ārthī bhāvanā) is expressed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) in its aspect as such. Now, what is this objective productive energy?

If it is argued that it is the "activity of the agent" (kartṛvyāpāra), we say no; for then even the sacrifice and so forth would result in being the productive energy, since they too are activities of the agent.

If it is argued that this is not an undesirable consequence because the sacrifice, being the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), cannot be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—to this they reply:
It is true that the sacrifice is not the *bhāvanā*; rather, the *bhāvanā* is the effort directed toward the sacrifice, which is produced by the desire for heaven.

And that very [effort] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātāṃśa*); for when one hears the verbal form "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there arises the cognition: "one strives by means of sacrifice.

Furthermore, because we observe the use of the verb "to do" (*karoti*) in such instances as "he performs walking and so forth," which are preceded by effort—where one says of someone who performs walking and so forth with effort, "he performs walking"—but we do not say "he performs shaking" when there is shaking caused by sacrifice and the like, but rather say "his shaking arises due to wind and so forth," it follows that the meaning of "to do" (*karoti*) is, at least in this context, effort (*prayatna*).
Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb "to do" (*karoti*) is observed in the case of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*):
"one should sacrifice" means "one should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice"; "he cooks" means "he effects cooking"; "he goes" means "he effects going.
And thus, because of this coreferentiality with "to do," effort (*prayatna*) is the denotation of the verbal suffix.

Nor should it be argued that the linguistic usage "the chariot goes" is untenable because there is no effort (*yatna*) in the chariot; for such usage is tenable by attributing to the chariot the effort residing in the horse that draws it. Even in the view where *bhāvanā* is defined as a general activity (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*) conducive to the production of another thing, since no activity conducive to motion is perceived in the chariot, the usage "the chariot goes" is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).
Therefore, effort alone is the objective *bhāvanā*.
As some have said:

"But it cannot be said that the efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) is prompted by effort, since what is under discussion here is that which is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Thus they desist.
Others, however, say:
Bhāvanā is the activity of the agent (bhāvaka) that is conducive to the becoming (bhavitṛ);
that is to say, it is such an activity that, once performed, renders the instrument capable of producing the result. And that alone is the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta).
For upon hearing the verbal form "he cuts with an axe," such a cognition arises:
"One should employ the axe in that activity by the performance of which cutting occurs through the axe. In the same way, the meaning of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" is as follows.
One should engage in that activity by means of which, once performed, heaven arises from the sacrifice.

That activity is, in some cases, such as raising and lowering [the sacrificial ladle], and in others, beginning with the kindling of the fires and ending with the satiation of the Brahmins. While it is understood subsequently through its specific qualifications when there is an expectancy regarding the "manner of being" (*kathaṃbhāva*), it is understood in a general sense—namely, as being conducive to the production of something else—from the verbal suffix itself.

Even in the sentence "the chariot goes to the village," it is the activity conducive to the attainment of the village that is understood by the verb (*ākhyāta*). This is because of the cognition that "the chariot is engaged in such a movement—that activity, when performed, results in the attainment of the village through going.
However, mere going is not the meaning of the verb here, as that has already been expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*).
When the question arises as to what that activity is, it is subsequently understood to be the aforementioned separation from one location and conjunction with another.

Just as from the usage "the chariot goes to the village" [it is understood that] having divided [itself] by the front part and joined [itself] with the rear part, so too in the case of "Devadatta exerts effort," Devadatta acts in such a way that effort (*prayatna*) comes to be; thus, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply the activity (*vyāpāra*) conducive to effort, and not the effort itself, because that is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). And when there is a requirement for a specific kind of activity, desire (*icchā*) and so forth are understood subsequently, just like the raising and lowering [of an axe].

And thus, because it is present everywhere, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is simply the general category of activity conducive to the production of another thing, and not mere effort alone; for that [effort] is absent in such cases as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*) or "Devadatta exerts himself" (*devadattaḥ prayatate*). Nor is it proper to claim that this [meaning] is figurative here, since it is improper to resort to a figurative sense when a primary one is possible. Even the meaning of the root *√kṛ* ("to do") is precisely an activity conducive to the production of another thing, and not mere effort, because *√kṛ* stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with verbal suffixes whose agents are both sentient and insentient.

Thus it is established that the "efficient force" (*arthī bhāvanā*) is an operation conducive to the production of something else. And this very [force] is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).
When there is a requirement for an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), heaven and so forth are connected as the object to be brought about.
When there is a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), sacrifice and so forth are connected as the instrument; and rites such as the *pravāda* are connected as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Thus, because sacrifices and the like are enjoined by such injunctions as "one should sacrifice" with heaven and so forth as the intended goal, it is established that sacrifices and the like constitute *dharma*, since they are prescribed by the Veda with a specific purpose in view.
This very *dharma*, when performed with the same purpose for which it was enjoined, is the cause of that [result].
However, when performed with the intention of dedicating it to Śrī Govinda, it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Nor is there a lack of authoritative evidence for performing [actions] with the intention of offering them to Him:
"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī— perform all that as an offering unto Me."

Thus says the Smṛti; and its authority is established like that of the Smṛtis concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites, as explained at length elsewhere. "Where am I, of dull intellect, and where is this system approved by the Bhāṭṭas?
Therefore, this is merely a manifestation of devotion toward the feet of my teacher Govinda."
"May Lord Govinda, who is affectionate toward his devotees, be pleased by this most beautiful verbal activity of mine in the form of this book.
Thus ends the Mīmāṃsā treatise named *Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa*, composed by Apadeva, the son of the illustrious Anantadeva.
